aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-00.text: Consider a sunset. You judge it beautiful at once, without any training or reasoning.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-01.text: Such a verdict is called a judgement of taste. Philosophers have asked what grounds these judgements for three hundred years.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-02.text: Two questions follow. What makes this pleasure distinctive, and for whom does the judgement speak?

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-03.text: Immanuel Kant contrasted beauty with appetite. When you’re hungry, you take an apple because you want to eat it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-04.text: The sunset satisfies no appetite. You want nothing from it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-05.text: Kant calls such pleasure disinterested, meaning free of desire. It doesn’t depend on wanting to use or possess the object.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-06.text: David Hume held that beauty is no quality in things, and exists only in the mind. Yet he ranked masters above hacks.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-07.text: Hume placed the standard of taste in the joint verdict of true critics. Practice, comparison and freedom from prejudice make their verdicts converge.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-08.text: The proposal risks circularity. A true critic is recognised by sound verdicts, yet sound verdicts are defined as those of true critics.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-11.text: The second question concerns whom a judgement of taste speaks for. You rarely stop at saying “I like it”.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-12.text: You say “it is beautiful”, as though stating a fact about the object. Yet the judgement rests only on your feeling of pleasure.

aesthetics-aesthetics-1/beat-13.text: Kant holds that it still speaks with a universal voice, and demands the agreement of everyone.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-00.text: Suppose a film is made with the greatest skill. Every frame is composed by a master.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-01.text: Yet all that skill is used to make cruelty look glorious.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-02.text: The verdict on its craft is uncontroversial. A second question concerns what the film asks you to feel.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-03.text: Autonomism holds that art should be judged on its craft alone. Oscar Wilde rules the second question out of aesthetic judgement.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-05.text: Moralism rejects the restriction. For the moralist, what a work invites you to feel is part of the work itself.

aesthetics-aesthetics-10/beat-06.text: A third position, ethicism, connects the two questions. Berys Gaut holds that a work inviting a response you shouldn’t have is, to that extent, flawed as art.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-00.text: Suppose a gallery hangs two pictures. One was painted by a person over four months.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-01.text: The other was generated by a machine in about nine seconds.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-02.text: The two pictures aren’t merely similar but identical.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-03.text: Every mark is in the same place, at the same size, in the same colour.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-04.text: Only the plaques tell the two apart. With the plaques covered, no visitor, curator or critic could reliably sort them.

aesthetics-aesthetics-11/beat-06.text: So every visible property is shared. What sets the two apart lies not in the objects but in how each was made.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-00.text: Suppose a poem is posted in a public square for anyone to read. The poet claims that every reader has misread the poem.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-01.text: A reader concludes the poem expresses grief. The image of a lamp left burning for someone, now gone out, supports the reading.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-02.text: Nothing in the text of the poem suggests irony or a joke.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-03.text: Every reader who studies the poem reaches the same reading. What the poet meant, however, is private and can’t be checked.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-05.text: The poet now insists that the last line was meant as a joke. Yet two more readers examine the poem and reach the same reading.

aesthetics-aesthetics-12/beat-06.text: Wimsatt and Beardsley called appeals like this the intentional fallacy. It treats the author’s intention as the standard of a poem’s meaning.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-00.text: Suppose two canvases hang side by side and look identical. One is a Vermeer.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-01.text: The other is a forgery painted last year. Han van Meegeren’s 1937 fake fooled Abraham Bredius, a leading expert.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-02.text: By hypothesis, no visible feature tells the two canvases apart. No amount of close inspection reveals which is genuine.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-03.text: The difference lies in provenance, the history of each canvas from the moment it was made. The Vermeer’s history runs back three and a half centuries.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-04.text: The forgery’s history begins last year, with the forger who painted it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-13/beat-06.text: When van Meegeren confessed in 1945, the canvases themselves did not change. Yet paintings once hailed as masterpieces were soon dismissed as forgeries.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-00.text: Suppose everyone in a room tastes the wine from one cask. Their verdict is unanimous.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-01.text: Every taster reports that there’s nothing wrong with the wine.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-02.text: Then two tasters dissent. One detects a faint taste of iron.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-03.text: The other finds the wine too sweet for their liking, a complaint of a different type.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-04.text: In 1757, David Hume published an essay on the standard of taste. It begins by granting that tastes vary widely.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-05.text: Yet Hume denies that every verdict is equally good. The joint verdict of true judges, he argues, is the standard of taste.

aesthetics-aesthetics-14/beat-07.text: Hume illustrates the point with a story from Cervantes’s Don Quixote. When the cask was emptied, a key on a leather thong lay at the bottom.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-00.text: Consider a rose and five sincere remarks a person might make about it. Each expresses a real attitude towards the flower.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-01.text: Immanuel Kant asks which one of the five is a judgement of beauty at all. The question isn’t which remark is true.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-02.text: Kant’s test is to set aside every personal stake in the rose. Kant calls such a stake an interest.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-03.text: A judgement of beauty is one whose delight survives when every interest is set aside.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-04.text: An interest is anything you want from the rose, such as owning it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-05.text: Selling the rose and decorating a room with it are interests too.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-06.text: So is the wish to impress someone by being seen with it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-09.text: Remove the four remarks with an interest, and the rose is unchanged. The remark left says more than that you like the rose.

aesthetics-aesthetics-15/beat-10.text: That remark addresses someone else. Kant holds that a judgement of beauty claims everyone’s agreement, as if beauty were in the rose.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-00.text: Suppose you’ve admired a painting on three visits, liking it more each time. Today you read the label beside it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-01.text: The painting was finished in 1911, and no mark on it has changed since.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-02.text: Whatever happens next happens to you, not to the canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-03.text: The label’s first line reports that the painter accepted the commission from a patron he despised. His own letter says so.

aesthetics-aesthetics-16/beat-05.text: The gallery adds more facts, until the label is longer than the painting is wide. Your attention shifts from the work to the biography.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-00.text: Suppose you see a shape in the dark. Your heart races, your skin goes cold, and you want to flee.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-01.text: Yet people pay to feel this fear at a horror film. They choose the racing heart and the cold skin.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-02.text: Framing the scene as fiction doesn’t reduce the fear. The physical response is as strong inside the frame as outside it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-04.text: Philosophers have offered three answers. For Aristotle, tragedy arouses pity and fear and brings about their catharsis, or purging.

aesthetics-aesthetics-17/beat-05.text: For Hume, the eloquence of the telling converts the fear into pleasure. For Noël Carroll, fear is the price paid for the pleasure of discovery.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-00.text: Consider a piece of music that listeners call sad. Its melody is slow, low in pitch and falling.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-01.text: A person who has had bad news shows the same contour. Their posture is slow, low and falling.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-02.text: This is the resemblance theory. Music sounds sad because its contour is like the way sad people move.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-03.text: The theory must admit a difficulty. A contour is not a mood, and no one in the notes feels sad.

aesthetics-aesthetics-18/beat-06.text: A second puzzle concerns the listener. Why do people choose music that makes them feel sad?

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-00.text: Aesthetics has long studied art. In 1966, Ronald Hepburn argued that it had neglected the beauty of nature.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-01.text: Consider a drainpipe. No one made it as art, yet it has a shape, a rhythm and a pattern of stains.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-02.text: Framing an object directs aesthetic attention to qualities that everyday use passes over.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-03.text: Now consider a marsh. It’s flat, full of insects, and offers no scenic view.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-04.text: Seen only as scenery, the marsh looks ugly. Allen Carlson calls this way of looking the landscape model, and rejects it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-06.text: Carlson brings in natural history instead. A marsh is a nursery, a water filter and a flood defence.

aesthetics-aesthetics-19/beat-07.text: Neither the frame nor the marsh has changed, yet the verdict on the marsh has.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-00.text: A painting can move you centuries after its painter has died. How can one person’s feeling reach another through paint?

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-01.text: The expression theory defines art by feeling, not by beauty or skill. Leo Tolstoy compared art to an infection that spreads a feeling to others.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-02.text: The artist feels an emotion, the work carries the emotion, and the audience feels it too. For Collingwood, artists discover their feelings only by expressing them.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-03.text: Tolstoy’s example is a boy who describes meeting a wolf and frightens his listeners. It’s art, provided the boy feels that fear again as he speaks.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-06.text: If the expression theory is right, a work of art embodies a feeling in lines, sounds or words.

aesthetics-aesthetics-2/beat-07.text: The feeling can then outlive its maker, and reach audiences in other languages and centuries.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-00.text: Consider four common reasons for valuing art. For each, ask whether something cheaper does the same job.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-01.text: First, art can teach. A textbook also teaches, often more quickly and with fewer mistakes.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-02.text: Second, art records how the world looked. A camera records appearances at least as faithfully.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-03.text: Third, wallpaper decorates a room more cheaply than art does.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-04.text: Each of the first three reasons has a cheaper substitute. No substitute has been found for the fourth.

aesthetics-aesthetics-20/beat-07.text: This method of elimination has a limit. Something can be replaceable and still be worth having.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-00.text: Consider three works of art. A novel exists in six printed copies, a symphony in four recordings, and a painting on one canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-01.text: Now suppose the six printed copies, the four recordings and the canvas are burnt. Which of the works still exist?

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-02.text: The novel and the symphony survive. The novel can be printed again from its text, and the symphony played again from its score.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-03.text: The painting cannot come back. A painting has no notation, such as a text or a score, from which to make another.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-04.text: The painting was the physical object itself. Nelson Goodman called such works autographic, and works like the novel allographic.

aesthetics-aesthetics-21/beat-07.text: Photography complicates the distinction. One negative can make many prints, yet collectors pay more for an early print.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-00.text: Kendall Walton describes a viewer, Charles, watching a horror film. A green slime oozes towards the camera, as if towards him.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-01.text: Charles’s heart rate rises and his muscles tense. His body responds as it would to a real danger.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-02.text: Yet Charles never believes that the slime exists. He knows he’s watching a film.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-03.text: The paradox of fiction consists of three claims that each seem true. First, you feel real fear at a film.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-04.text: Second, an emotion requires a belief that its object exists. Third, you don’t believe the film’s events are real.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-06.text: Walton rejects the first claim. On his view, Charles plays a game of make-believe, and only within the game does he fear the slime.

aesthetics-aesthetics-22/beat-08.text: The thought theory, held by Peter Lamarque and Noël Carroll, rejects the second claim instead. Vividly imagining a thing is enough to move you.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-00.text: A melody of seven notes has no words. Yet it can move a listener to tears.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-01.text: What, then, is the melody about? Music might mean something in two different ways.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-02.text: The first way is expression. Peter Kivy argues that a slow, falling melody sounds sad because it resembles a sad person’s bearing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-03.text: The second way is representation, which means being about something. Violins can imitate birdsong, but a title usually names the bird.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-05.text: Music that represents nothing is called absolute music. Most instrumental music is absolute in this sense.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-06.text: Such music has no subject beyond its own patterns of tones.

aesthetics-aesthetics-23/beat-08.text: Arthur Schopenhauer held that music does represent. It copies no visible thing, but the will hidden behind all things.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-00.text: Consider a painted panel that has hung in one room for five hundred years. Visitors travel across the world to stand before it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-01.text: A print, a poster, a screen and a feed reproduce the picture everywhere at once. Yet none of them occupies the original’s place.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-02.text: Walter Benjamin called what the copies lack the aura. It concerns a work’s unique presence in time and space, not its quality.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-04.text: An altarpiece stood in one church, and pilgrims travelled to see it. A film has no original print that viewers must travel to.

aesthetics-aesthetics-24/beat-06.text: Benjamin also saw a gain in this loss. Freed from ritual, a work can reach everybody and take on a political function.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-00.text: Taste in art feels personal. Yet the sociologist Pierre Bourdieu found that it closely tracks social class and upbringing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-01.text: Consider two visitors in front of the same canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-02.text: One recognises its style and subject at once. The other can’t tell what to look for.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-03.text: Bourdieu locates the difference in what each visitor brings to the canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-05.text: Bourdieu called such a background cultural capital. It includes books at home, gallery visits and conversation over meals.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-06.text: Cultural capital is acquired in childhood, so it feels like natural taste rather than training.

aesthetics-aesthetics-25/beat-08.text: Kant said a judgement of beauty is disinterested. Bourdieu replied that such detachment requires freedom from economic need.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-00.text: Consider a plastic flamingo on a lawn. By any ordinary standard it’s bad art, yet many people love it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-01.text: Kitsch is art that supplies ready-made emotion. A painted kitten with enormous wet eyes is a standard example.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-02.text: Milan Kundera wrote that kitsch brings two tears. The first is for children running on grass, the second for the pleasure of being moved.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-03.text: Camp is a different attitude. The lover of kitsch is sincere, while camp loves bad taste knowingly.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-05.text: Susan Sontag defined camp in 1964 as a love of the unnatural. Her examples include Tiffany lamps and Swan Lake.

aesthetics-aesthetics-26/beat-07.text: The same flamingo can be either kitsch or camp. One neighbour admires it sincerely, and another enjoys it as absurd.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-00.text: Over the twentieth century, some composers replaced melody with noise. One piece asked a pianist to play no notes at all.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-01.text: Such artists are called the avant-garde. The term is military and originally meant the advance guard of an army.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-02.text: Cubism gave up single-point perspective, and atonal music gave up the key. Dada sound poetry gave up words that meant anything.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-03.text: These artists held that habit dulls perception. You stop noticing what you see every day.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-05.text: At its premiere in 1952, John Cage’s piece had a pianist play no notes for four minutes and thirty-three seconds. The sounds in the hall became the music.

aesthetics-aesthetics-27/beat-07.text: Critics in 1874 mocked Impressionist paintings as unfinished sketches. Today they’re among the most widely reproduced paintings.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-00.text: Suppose you haven’t visited a museum in months. You may still have had aesthetic experiences every day this week.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-01.text: Examples include the smell of rain, a well-ordered desk and an unexpected pass in a football match.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-02.text: For centuries, aesthetics studied mainly the fine arts, such as painting, music and poetry. Most of a life happens elsewhere.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-03.text: Yuriko Saito argues that cooking, dressing, cleaning and commuting deserve aesthetic attention too. This field is called everyday aesthetics.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-05.text: A footballer makes a pass nobody expected, and the stadium gasps. The pass has grace, good timing and a form suited to its purpose.

aesthetics-aesthetics-28/beat-07.text: The view faces an objection. If a tidy drawer and a Rembrandt are both aesthetic, the word marks nothing special.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-00.text: Suppose you read a novel about a war that was never fought, with soldiers who never lived. You may still feel you learned something.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-01.text: A work of fiction describes events that didn’t happen. How, then, could it teach anything true?

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-02.text: Plato would banish poets from his ideal city. Poetry, he argued, imitates appearances and stirs feeling against reason.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-03.text: A psychology textbook can tell you that grief exists. A novel can show what grief is like from the inside.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-05.text: Suppose a reader finishes a war novel and says she now understands what soldiers endure.

aesthetics-aesthetics-29/beat-07.text: Jerome Stolnitz argued that fiction’s truths are trivial and unconfirmed. Its soldiers are invented, so nothing in the novel confirms what real soldiers feel.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-00.text: Every human culture on record has made music and told stories. No society studied by anthropologists lacks either.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-01.text: A practice found in every culture calls for an explanation. Why would people seek out stories that make them suffer?

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-02.text: Aristotle held that a tragedy arouses pity and fear in its audience, and then releases them.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-03.text: The effect is called katharsis, a term Aristotle never explained. Readers still disagree about what it means.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-04.text: In Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, Oedipus discovers that he has killed his own father. Aristotle calls this a recognition, a change from ignorance to knowledge.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-05.text: Aristotle also writes that people enjoy accurate images of painful things, because learning from them is a pleasure.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-07.text: Music can make you sad without giving you any reason to be sad. Arthur Schopenhauer held that music expresses the will, the blind striving behind everything in nature.

aesthetics-aesthetics-3/beat-08.text: Plato, over two thousand years earlier, argued that music shapes character before reason develops. So he thought music dangerous.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-00.text: Beauty seems inessential to survival. Food keeps a person alive, and shelter keeps them safe.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-01.text: What, then, is beauty for? One answer treats it as decoration, the first thing given up when life gets hard.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-02.text: Iris Murdoch gave a different answer. A hovering kestrel, she wrote, can end a person’s anxious brooding.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-03.text: Murdoch called the change unselfing. The brooding self disappears, and attention rests on something real.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-05.text: Visitors to Florence have reported dizziness and a racing heart in front of its art. Beauty can affect a person with physical force.

aesthetics-aesthetics-30/beat-07.text: For Murdoch, learning to attend properly to a bird is practice for attending properly to a person.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-00.text: Suppose a musician plays a phrase of nine notes on four strings. The audience is pleased by a good phrase, well played.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-01.text: The audience applauds politely, but no one stands.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-02.text: Now suppose three strings are removed, and the same nine notes are played on one. The tempo, phrasing and sound are identical to the first performance.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-04.text: This time the audience gives a standing ovation. Yet the sound reaching their ears is unchanged.

aesthetics-aesthetics-31/beat-05.text: Only the audience’s response has changed, so the extra applause must be for something other than the sound.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-00.text: Consider nine years of a life, with one bar for how well each year goes. This life begins badly and ends with its best years.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-01.text: The second chart contains the same nine years in the opposite order. It begins well and ends badly.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-02.text: The second life contains the same goods as the first, and only their order differs.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-03.text: A third life stays level, never bad and never remarkable. Its nine identical years add up to the same total as the other two.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-05.text: A line marks each life’s average year, and it sits at the same height in all three. Adding up well-being can’t tell the three lives apart.

aesthetics-aesthetics-32/beat-06.text: The additive view holds that a life’s value is the sum of the well-being in its years. Yet the three lives don’t seem equally good.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-00.text: Consider a painting four hundred years old, never cleaned. The surface has darkened, and the details are hard to make out.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-01.text: The surface is a stack of layers. Paint lies at the bottom, then the painter’s thin glaze, then varnish, then centuries of smoke and dust.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-02.text: Removing the dirt is uncontroversial. Dirt isn’t part of the work, because the painter didn’t put it there.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-03.text: Beyond the dirt, restorers disagree. In the 1980s, cleaning the Sistine Chapel ceiling revealed bright pinks and greens.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-04.text: James Beck, an art historian, argued that Michelangelo’s own final glazes had been removed. The restorers answered that the dark layer was soot and wax from candles.

aesthetics-aesthetics-33/beat-07.text: The rule “return it to the original” doesn’t settle the question. Nothing shows which layer the painter put on last.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-00.text: Consider a bull drawn in eleven strokes. Anyone can recognise the animal without being told what it is.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-01.text: What makes this a picture of a bull? Nelson Goodman argues that resemblance is not enough, since twins look alike and neither pictures the other.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-02.text: Now suppose the strokes are removed one by one. Between 1945 and 1946, Pablo Picasso reworked one lithograph of a bull through eleven stages, each simpler than the last.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-03.text: The final stage is a few lines, yet still unmistakably a bull. If more strokes were removed, no one could say which stage would first fail to depict a bull.

aesthetics-aesthetics-34/beat-06.text: So convention and context do most of the work. You’ve learned the usual way to draw a bull, and three lines are enough to recognise the animal.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-00.text: The setup of a joke leads you along one reading, like a train on a single track. You come to expect a particular ending.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-01.text: The setup line reads, “I told my doctor I broke my arm in two places.”

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-02.text: On the natural reading, the two places are points on the arm, and you’re waiting for a diagnosis.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-04.text: The incongruity theory says a joke is funny because it breaks what you expect. But both readings must still fit the same words.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-05.text: A punchline that fits no reading of the setup is an error, not a surprise.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-07.text: Suppose the second reading is shown before the punchline arrives. The words and the switch are the same, but the joke is no longer funny.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-08.text: Explaining a joke reveals the second reading in advance, and so removes the surprise.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-09.text: Thomas Hobbes held that you laugh when you suddenly feel above someone. His superiority theory explains only some jokes.

aesthetics-aesthetics-35/beat-10.text: Sigmund Freud’s relief theory holds that a joke releases energy normally used to repress the feelings it expresses.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-00.text: Consider one square on one afternoon. A dense crowd fills one end, and a single man stands at the other.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-01.text: Everything in the square is real, and none of it will be altered.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-03.text: Neither print has been manipulated, since no pixel was moved, added or removed.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-04.text: Both prints are accurate, yet they imply opposite accounts of what happened.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-05.text: Photographs have this power because they’re made mechanically, by light from the scene itself.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-06.text: Kendall Walton argues that photographs are transparent: through them, you literally see the square itself.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-09.text: A painting misleads less by framing, because no viewer assumes a painting is neutral. Everyone knows a painter made choices.

aesthetics-aesthetics-36/beat-10.text: With a photograph, viewers easily forget that a photographer also made choices.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-00.text: Consider two performances. The upper piece was written in advance, so every note existed before anyone came on stage.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-01.text: The lower row is an improvised solo. Each note is decided as it’s played, with no score to compare it against.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-03.text: A symphony isn’t its score, so you can burn every copy of a symphony and it survives. An unrecorded solo ends when the playing stops.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-05.text: Recording changed this. Players began learning famous solos note for note, so an event meant to happen once acquired a correct version.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-07.text: The same sounds can be two different kinds of thing, depending on whether a composition preceded them.

aesthetics-aesthetics-37/beat-08.text: The difference lies not in how the music sounds, but in what the music is.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-00.text: Suppose you watch a thriller for the second time. You already know that the hero escapes the building.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-01.text: In every scene, what you know is complete from the first frame. Yet what you feel still rises.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-02.text: The paradox of suspense sets out three claims that can’t all be true. You know the ending, you’re still tense, and suspense requires doubt.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-04.text: The puzzle is old. Greek tragedies usually retold traditional myths, whose outcomes were fixed before the play began.

aesthetics-aesthetics-38/beat-05.text: Samuel Taylor Coleridge described engagement with fiction as a willing act, not a lapse of memory.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-00.text: A chair and a sculpture can be made from the same wood, by the same hands, with the same skill. So materials and skill can’t separate art from craft.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-01.text: The difference, then, must lie in the making. Each route runs from a plan at the top, through the hours of work beneath it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-02.text: Each route ends in a finished work: a chair, a poem and a copy.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-04.text: R. G. Collingwood draws his line between art and craft in the process of making, not in the finished object.

aesthetics-aesthetics-39/beat-05.text: Immanuel Kant drew a related line in 1790. He placed the difference between art and handicraft in freedom.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-00.text: In 1917, a mass-produced urinal was submitted to an art exhibition. It wasn’t carved or painted, only chosen.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-01.text: The case raises a question of definition. What makes any object a work of art?

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-02.text: Two older theories answer it. The first, from Plato and Aristotle, holds that art is skilled imitation, or mimesis.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-03.text: The second, from Tolstoy, holds that art expresses a feeling and conveys it to an audience. Both theories assume someone made the work.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-04.text: Marcel Duchamp turned the urinal on its back, signed it with the name “R. Mutt 1917”, and titled the work Fountain.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-05.text: The exhibition’s board refused to display the work. An unsigned defence argued that whether Mutt made it with his own hands had no importance.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-06.text: The defence held that choosing was the artistic act. Placed under a new title, the object lost its everyday use.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-08.text: Fountain copies nothing and expresses no feeling, so neither theory fits. For George Dickie, the institutions of the artworld make it art.

aesthetics-aesthetics-4/beat-09.text: Asking whether something is art is philosophical. It forces you to state the definition you privately hold.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-00.text: Galleries hang paintings, not dinners. Philosophers have long given a reason for the difference.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-01.text: G. W. F. Hegel divided the senses into two groups. Sight and hearing, he held, can carry art.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-02.text: Smell, taste and touch were excluded, a division already discussed by Plato.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-03.text: Looking leaves a painting intact, but eating consumes a dinner. Hegel held that works of art must keep their independence from the viewer.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-05.text: Consider a tasting menu. It opens, develops a theme, alludes to an older dish and concludes.

aesthetics-aesthetics-40/beat-07.text: Diners argue about whether the fifth course earned its place. That’s following a form.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-00.text: Suppose you point at the edge of a painting. Is your finger on the painting or off it?

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-01.text: The canvas belongs to the work, and the wall belongs to the room. The frame is the difficult case.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-02.text: Immanuel Kant called such things parerga, things beside the work. Frames on pictures and the clothing on statues are his examples.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-03.text: A frame is not part of the painting. The painting would be the same painting without one.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-05.text: The frame is not outside the work either. A gilt frame and a steel frame change how the same canvas is seen.

aesthetics-aesthetics-41/beat-07.text: The boundary problem extends outward, to the title, the wall label, the hanging height and the museum itself.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-00.text: You look at the world all day, yet rarely attend to it closely. Iris Murdoch and John Ruskin both treated such attention as a skill.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-01.text: Murdoch borrowed the concept of attention from Simone Weil. Attention is a just and loving look at one real thing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-02.text: Murdoch calls the obstacle “the fat relentless ego”, a self absorbed in its own concerns. Attention draws the mind away from it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-03.text: Murdoch describes gazing out of a window, brooding on a blow to her prestige, when she sees a kestrel.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-04.text: The brooding self is lost for a moment, and only the kestrel remains. Murdoch calls this unselfing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-07.text: John Ruskin wrote that painting depends on recovering “the innocence of the eye”. The innocent eye sees flat patches of colour before the mind names them.

aesthetics-aesthetics-5/beat-08.text: Ruskin’s drawing exercises therefore begin with a single leaf, and only later reach a whole tree.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-00.text: A vast mountain or a storm at sea can frighten you. Why, then, do people seek out such sights for pleasure?

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-01.text: In 1757, Edmund Burke distinguished two aesthetic responses. The beautiful, like a flower, is small, smooth and pleasing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-02.text: The sublime, like a vast mountain, is rugged and overwhelming. It produces a delight mixed with terror.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-03.text: Suppose you stand on a cliff in a gale. The drop could kill you, but you’re well back from the edge.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-04.text: Burke argued that danger seen from a safe distance is delightful. He distinguished this delight from the positive pleasure of beauty.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-07.text: Immanuel Kant placed the sublime in the mind rather than in nature. A mountain overwhelms the imagination, which can’t take in its size.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-08.text: Yet reason can think the infinite as a whole, where the imagination fails. The mountain is not the sublime thing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-6/beat-09.text: Sublimity lies in your awareness that your reason is superior to nature.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-00.text: Suppose a friend judges a scribble better than a masterwork. You may want to call the verdict mistaken.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-01.text: The difficulty is to say on what grounds, if beauty is a matter of feeling.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-02.text: One work took three seconds to make, and the other took thirty years of practice.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-03.text: Nearly all visitors prefer the masterwork, and only a few the scribble. Yet popularity doesn’t make a verdict correct.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-04.text: David Hume held that beauty isn’t a property of the object at all. No measurement of the canvas will find it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-05.text: Beauty, for Hume, is a sentiment, a feeling that arises in the mind of the viewer.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-07.text: If beauty is only a feeling, your friend’s feeling seems as valid as anyone’s. The scribble would then tie with the masterwork.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-08.text: Hume rejected the tie. Ranking the minor poet Ogilby equal to Milton, he wrote, is like calling a molehill as high as a mountain.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-10.text: Hume listed the qualities of a true critic. They include practice, comparison, freedom from prejudice and good sense.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-11.text: Hume holds that the joint verdict of such critics is the standard of taste.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-12.text: The standard isn’t snobbery. A trained wine taster detects flavours a novice can’t, because practice reshapes perception itself.

aesthetics-aesthetics-7/beat-13.text: If you return after studying many works, you’ll perceive more in this canvas than you do today.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-00.text: Two people admire the same painting. One says it succeeds because of how its shapes are arranged.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-01.text: The other says it succeeds because it expresses a feeling. Both are judging the same canvas.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-02.text: Each reason corresponds to a different theory of what makes art valuable.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-03.text: Each view can be pictured as a pair of glasses, and a pair for each hangs on the wall. Consider the first pair.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-04.text: The glasses change nothing in the painting. They change which of its features you attend to.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-05.text: Through the first pair, the painting is pure arrangement. What matters is how blocks, edges and shapes relate to one another.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-06.text: What the picture represents plays no part in this way of seeing.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-07.text: A second pair of glasses hangs on the same wall, for the second viewer.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-08.text: This pair picks out different features, so the same canvas presents a different painting.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-09.text: Through the second pair, the blocks dissolve into expressive strokes. Proportions and edges no longer matter.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-10.text: What matters now is the feeling the strokes convey, as if the painter had passed on a mood.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-12.text: The first way of looking is called formalism. Clive Bell claimed that all genuine works of visual art share a single quality.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-13.text: Bell called it significant form, an arrangement of lines and colours that stirs aesthetic emotion. Subject matter is irrelevant.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-15.text: The second way of looking is the expression theory. Tolstoy held that art transmits a feeling from one person to others.

aesthetics-aesthetics-8/beat-16.text: Collingwood developed a different version. A painter, he held, often discovers the feeling only in the act of painting.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-00.text: For centuries, philosophers and critics treated beauty as the defining mark of art.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-01.text: On this view, beauty is a necessary condition, so a work without beauty couldn’t count as art.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-02.text: In 1964, Andy Warhol exhibited plywood boxes painted to look like Brillo soap-pad cartons.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-03.text: Warhol’s work copied an ordinary commercial package rather than anything beautiful.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-04.text: Arthur Danto posed the problem of indiscernibles. Two objects can look identical, yet only one is a work of art.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-05.text: One box is in a supermarket and one is in a gallery. Perception alone can’t tell you which is the artwork.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-07.text: So the difference is not in the object. For Danto, the difference lies in the work’s meaning and in the art history behind it.

aesthetics-aesthetics-9/beat-08.text: Beauty remains possible in art, but it no longer decides what counts as art.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-00.text: You claim to know many things. But what separates knowing something from merely believing it?

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-01.text: Epistemology is the branch of philosophy that studies knowledge. Plato examined this question in his dialogue the Theaetetus.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-02.text: The traditional analysis sets three conditions for knowledge. The first is truth: what you believe must be true.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-03.text: The second is belief: you must accept the claim. The third is justification: you must have good reasons for it.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-04.text: A belief that meets all three conditions is knowledge. Each condition is necessary, and the three together are sufficient.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-05.text: Without the third condition, a true belief could be held for no reason at all. It would then be correct only by luck.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-06.text: Justification is meant to connect a belief to the truth, so that being right isn’t a matter of luck.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-07.text: In the Theaetetus, Socrates describes jurors persuaded by skilled speakers. Their verdict is true, but they never witnessed what happened.

epistemology-knowledge-1/beat-08.text: The jurors believe what’s true. But being persuaded is no good reason, so the jurors lack knowledge.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-00.text: You aren’t absolutely certain that the sun will rise tomorrow. Even so, you’d bet heavily that it will.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-01.text: Can you know that the sun will rise without being certain of it?

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-02.text: One old answer, called infallibilism, says you know something only if you couldn’t be wrong. Held strictly, that rules out almost everything, even the sunrise and your own name.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-03.text: Fallibilism, a term introduced by Charles Sanders Peirce, rejects that standard. You can know something even though you might be wrong.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-04.text: On this view, knowledge is compatible with the possibility of error.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-06.text: Science shows that knowledge and fallibility can coexist. Its theories stay open to revision, yet science has produced a great deal of knowledge.

epistemology-knowledge-10/beat-07.text: As new evidence arrives, confidence in a theory rises or falls. Such revision is part of scientific method, not a sign of its failure.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-00.text: Suppose you glance at the hallway clock and it reads three o’clock. The time is in fact three o’clock.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-01.text: Your belief that it’s three o’clock is true. But do you know the time?

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-02.text: A little later, the real time has moved on. The hallway clock still reads three.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-03.text: The hallway clock stopped at three o’clock, twelve hours before you looked. Bertrand Russell gave this example in 1948.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-04.text: The traditional account defines knowledge as justified true belief. First, you believed that it was three o’clock.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-05.text: Second, the belief was true. Third, it was justified, since reading a clock is an ordinary way to learn the time.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-06.text: Your belief therefore meets all three conditions: belief, truth and justification.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-08.text: The stopped clock matched the real time only at the moment you happened to look. So your belief was true by luck.

epistemology-knowledge-11/beat-09.text: Nothing connected your reason to the fact that made the belief true. A match of this kind is called epistemic luck.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-00.text: You’ve never seen an atom, and you don’t remember being born. Yet you’re confident of both facts.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-01.text: By what routes do beliefs like these reach you?

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-02.text: The first source is perception, the most direct. Rain lands on your hand, and you believe it’s raining without inferring anything.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-03.text: Memory is the second source. You still know what you ate this morning, although the toast is gone, because memory preserves what you perceived.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-04.text: A remembered belief travels a longer route, because it must be stored and later recalled.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-06.text: The third source, testimony, begins with other people. It reaches you from teachers, books, mapmakers and writers long dead.

epistemology-knowledge-12/beat-07.text: Most of what you know reaches you by testimony rather than by your own observation.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-00.text: Suppose a fair lottery has a million tickets and a single winner. You hold ticket forty thousand and one.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-01.text: At odds of a million to one, believing that your ticket will lose seems rational.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-02.text: Twenty tickets stand in for the million. The argument is the same for any number of tickets.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-03.text: At a million to one, you believe the first ticket will lose. The belief is still not certain, yet it’s better supported than much ordinary knowledge.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-05.text: The same reasoning applies to every ticket, so each belief that a ticket will lose is justified.

epistemology-knowledge-13/beat-06.text: Together, the verdicts imply that no ticket wins, yet you know one ticket will. Henry Kyburg set out this lottery paradox in 1961.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-00.text: Indirect realism holds that you perceive the world only through your experience of it. A leap separates what you see from the world.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-01.text: Every check you make on a belief relies on your own experience. So every check happens on this side of the screen, never against the world itself.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-02.text: On this view, the world is not something you observe but something you infer. You reason to it across the leap, from what appears on the screen.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-04.text: Now suppose your brain were kept in a vat, and a computer supplied all your experiences. This is the brain-in-a-vat scenario.

epistemology-knowledge-14/beat-05.text: What appears on the screen doesn’t change. Every experience in the vat would match an experience in the world.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-00.text: Two questions can be asked of anything you know. First, could you know it before looking, or only after?

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-01.text: Second, does it add something to what you know, or only unpack a definition?

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-02.text: You know that bachelors are unmarried before looking, by unpacking a word. Kant calls such a truth analytic and a priori.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-03.text: You know that the chair is over there only after looking, and it adds something. Kant calls such a truth synthetic and a posteriori.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-04.text: An empiricist rule, traced to David Hume, holds that the synthetic a priori box is empty. If you did not have to look, you learned nothing new.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-05.text: Put the other way, anything that adds to your knowledge can be known only after looking.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-07.text: Kant argues that the synthetic a priori box isn’t empty. His example is the truth that seven plus five is twelve.

epistemology-knowledge-15/beat-08.text: You need no experiment to know it, so it’s a priori. Yet, Kant argues, the concept of twelve isn’t contained in seven, five and addition, so it’s synthetic.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-00.text: During the total eclipse of 1919, astronomers measured how much starlight bends near the sun. The result could have been none, or any amount.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-01.text: Each of three theories is drawn as wide as the results it permits. Two permit only a narrow range, so they forbid almost every result.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-02.text: The third permits every possible result, so any measurement would have fitted it.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-03.text: Karl Popper argued that this apparent strength is in fact a weakness.

epistemology-knowledge-16/beat-05.text: The results matched Einstein’s prediction of about one and three-quarter seconds of arc. His theory survived, and the prediction of half that bend was refuted.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-00.text: A scientific theory places a frame around the facts it explains. Inside the frame, those facts fit what the theory expects.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-01.text: Some results don’t fit the theory. These are anomalies, and scientists rarely abandon a theory because of them.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-02.text: Instead, they adjust the theory to absorb each anomaly. Ptolemaic astronomers, for example, kept adjusting their system of circles.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-03.text: Thomas Kuhn based his account on the history of science. Most of science is not testing the frame.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-04.text: Kuhn calls this work within the frame normal science. He calls the frame itself a paradigm.

epistemology-knowledge-17/beat-06.text: Then a revolution replaces the whole paradigm. Copernicus put the sun at the centre, and the facts took a new order without one of them moving.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-00.text: Consider two claims: the earth is round, and your keys are in the drawer. You believe the first far more firmly than the second.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-01.text: The claim that the earth is round is supported by almost everything else you know.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-02.text: The claim about your keys rests on a single memory of putting them there.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-03.text: Now suppose the same evidence arrives against both. Someone you trust tells you that each claim is false.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-04.text: The same report shouldn’t move both beliefs the same distance. How far a belief moves depends on more than the report.

epistemology-knowledge-18/beat-06.text: Bayesian reasoning, named after Thomas Bayes, makes this exact. The same evidence barely moves a belief you’re nearly sure of, but it can overturn a weak one.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-00.text: Each of five experts knows a subject that you don’t: engines, the heart, nutrition, tax law and the climate.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-01.text: Expertise is a relation between a person and a subject. The question “is this diet safe?” fits only one of these doors.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-02.text: Consider a common failure. A famous heart doctor is asked about diet on television, and gives an answer.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-03.text: The doctor’s credentials are genuine, and nobody has lied.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-04.text: But the credentials concern the heart, not nutrition. That doesn’t make the answer authoritative on its own.

epistemology-knowledge-19/beat-07.text: A harder case arises when two people behind the right door, both qualified, give opposite answers.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-00.text: Suppose you’ve read every word ever written about swimming, its physics, technique and breathing.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-01.text: Does all that reading, on its own, make you able to swim?

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-02.text: Consider the instruction “keep the head low”. It’s precise, true and easy to check.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-03.text: Every instruction serves an end beyond itself. Here the end is the doing, the act of swimming.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-04.text: The full method adds more instructions, and you’ve memorised every one. Gilbert Ryle calls knowledge of such facts knowing that.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-05.text: Even so, the box underneath stays empty. The ability to swim, which Ryle calls knowing how, hasn’t arrived.

epistemology-knowledge-2/beat-07.text: The box fills only through practice. Ryle holds that knowing how is distinct from knowing that.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-00.text: Suppose one source reports a surprising claim. With only one source, it’s reasonable to believe it tentatively.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-01.text: Then three more sources report the same claim: a paper, a friend and a podcast.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-02.text: Your confidence rises, and rightly so: four independent confirmations would be strong evidence.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-03.text: But three of the four sources are repeating the same original post.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-04.text: No source has retracted its claim, and all four still agree.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-05.text: Yet there were never four independent sources, only two: one post and one reporter’s own legwork.

epistemology-knowledge-20/beat-08.text: A social media feed favours posts shared by people like you. So the agreement in a feed often looks independent when it isn’t.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-00.text: Try, right now, to believe that it’s raining outside. Imagining rain, or saying that it’s raining, doesn’t count.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-01.text: Doxastic voluntarism is the view that you can believe something just by deciding to. This attempt puts the view to the test.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-02.text: The needle shows how strongly you believe that it’s raining. At present it rests against doubt.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-03.text: Two kinds of input might move the needle: acts of will and evidence.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-04.text: The first tray holds acts of will, beginning with a strong desire that it be raining.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-05.text: Add a firm decision to believe it, and the words “it’s raining” repeated to yourself.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-06.text: Add a large reward for believing it. The tray fills and the needle does not move.

epistemology-knowledge-21/beat-08.text: Now put one item in the evidence tray: rain on the window. With no act of will at all, the needle swings to belief.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-00.text: Suppose two people want to reach the same address. The first asks someone who knows the way.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-01.text: The second person has no information and guesses the way.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-02.text: Both arrive, and both now hold a true belief. This raises the value problem: why is knowledge worth more?

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-03.text: Yet the two routes differ. The first person’s route is a road that can be travelled again.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-04.text: The guesser’s route is a row of stepping stones with gaps between them.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-06.text: In the Meno, Plato compares true opinions to the statues of Daedalus, which run away unless tied down. Once tied down by reasoning, Plato says, they become knowledge.

epistemology-knowledge-22/beat-08.text: So the extra value is not in today at all. It lies in stability over time, which a lucky guess lacks.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-00.text: Virtue epistemology studies the traits of a good thinker. Model a mind as a sieve: the claims that reach its tray are what you believe.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-01.text: Open-mindedness widens the mouth, so more claims get a hearing. Nothing about that decides how much you keep.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-02.text: Intellectual rigour tightens the mesh, so fewer claims survive scrutiny. The mouth stays as wide as before.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-04.text: With the mouth closed, the mesh has no claims to test. Such a thinker admits no new errors, and no new truths either.

epistemology-knowledge-23/beat-06.text: So intellectual virtue needs both settings at once. Openness without rigour is credulity, and rigour without openness is dogmatism.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-00.text: Consider a sceptical argument about dreaming, set out step by step. Each step follows validly from the ones before it.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-01.text: Beside each claim, a bar shows how certain you are that it’s true. The bar measures credibility, not how persuasive the claim sounds.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-02.text: The bars rate the premise that you can’t rule out a dream highest. They rate the sceptic’s conclusion lowest.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-03.text: Moore held up his hand and said he knew this was a hand. That claim is more credible than any claim on the ladder.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-06.text: A valid argument can also be run in reverse. You should reject a premise when you’re surer the conclusion is false than the premises are true.

epistemology-knowledge-24/beat-07.text: The sceptic can reply that the bar measures confidence, not knowledge. Whether Moore knows he has a hand is the very point in dispute.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-00.text: Suppose you adopt a criterion, a test for what counts as knowledge. How could you check that the criterion itself is correct?

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-01.text: Checking the criterion requires a second criterion, used as a ruler for the first. That second ruler needs checking too.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-02.text: Each check calls for a further check, so the series has no last member. The result is an infinite regress.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-03.text: Sextus Empiricus argued that no criterion can be established. The checks either run on for ever or return in a circle.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-05.text: A methodist starts with a criterion and uses it to sort beliefs. Roderick Chisholm’s example is John Locke’s empiricism.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-06.text: A particularist reverses the order. Particular cases of knowledge come first, and a criterion is built to fit them.

epistemology-knowledge-25/beat-08.text: Neither starting point can be proved without assuming it. Chisholm conceded that every answer to the problem begs the question.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-00.text: Suppose you and a friend each work out your share of a restaurant bill. You get forty-three.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-01.text: Your friend gets forty-five. Both of you are careful, and both are good at arithmetic.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-02.text: Your friend is therefore an epistemic peer: someone with the same evidence and the same competence as you.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-03.text: So you can’t assume that she made the mistake. As your peer, she’s as likely to be right as you are.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-05.text: The disagreement is itself a piece of evidence. Conciliationists like David Christensen say you should become less sure.

epistemology-knowledge-26/beat-07.text: The steadfast view, defended by Thomas Kelly, holds that a well-reasoned belief may stand. Otherwise anyone who disagrees could force a retreat.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-00.text: You can wrong somebody without telling a single lie. Doubting a speaker because of prejudice can be enough.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-01.text: Suppose a patient gives a doctor an accurate account of her symptoms.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-02.text: The doctor treats the report as anxiety, because the patient is young. Her word receives less credit than it’s owed.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-03.text: Miranda Fricker calls this testimonial injustice. Prejudice makes a hearer give a speaker too little credibility.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-05.text: Fricker names a second wrong, hermeneutical injustice. Here a group lacks the shared concepts to make sense of its experience.

epistemology-knowledge-27/beat-07.text: Victims of sexual harassment had no shared concept for the wrong until the term was coined in the 1970s.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-00.text: Reasoning can work like a scientist testing a theory, or like a lawyer defending a verdict already chosen.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-01.text: Suppose a study finds your favourite habit harmful. You examine the sample size, the method and the funding.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-02.text: A second study of equal quality finds the habit harmless. You accept the result and share it without checking further.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-03.text: The evidence is of equal quality, but the standards differ. Your preference, not the data, set the standard.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-05.text: Motivated reasoning feels like being right from the inside, which is why it is hard to detect.

epistemology-knowledge-28/beat-07.text: In motivated reasoning the conclusion comes first, and reasons are gathered afterwards to support it.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-00.text: You can memorise every fact on the page and understand none of it.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-01.text: Consider two cooks who both know a recipe word for word. When the sauce splits, one of them can’t save it.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-02.text: The other cook saves it at once. Both know the same facts, but only the second understands why the recipe works.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-03.text: Understanding is knowing why. Grasping how facts explain one another lets understanding extend to new cases.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-05.text: Suppose a student passes a physics test by memorising the answers. She can’t solve a problem she hasn’t seen.

epistemology-knowledge-29/beat-07.text: Every fact she holds is true, but the facts are unconnected. Nothing in them lets her apply them to a new case.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-00.text: Can you be wrong about something you feel certain of? René Descartes set out to doubt his beliefs, to find a firm foundation for knowledge.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-01.text: The question rests on a distinction between certainty and truth. Feeling certain is something happening in you.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-02.text: Truth is a matter of how the world is. Since certainty can accompany a false belief, Descartes seeks beliefs that withstand every possible doubt.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-03.text: Descartes supposes an evil demon who uses all its power to deceive him. His senses, his memories and even simple sums could then be false.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-04.text: Descartes resolves to treat every belief that could possibly be false as if it were false.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-06.text: Descartes does not believe the demon exists. The supposition is a test: of each belief, he asks whether a deceiver could mislead him about it.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-07.text: Nearly every belief fails this test. One survives, the belief “I exist”, because a deceiver needs someone to deceive.

epistemology-knowledge-3/beat-08.text: Used as a method, doubt is constructive. It removes uncertain beliefs to reach a foundation on which knowledge can be rebuilt.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-00.text: Most of epistemology asks what knowledge is and how beliefs are justified.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-01.text: Virtue epistemology asks a further question: what makes someone a good knower?

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-02.text: A wise knower isn’t the one holding the most facts. Wisdom depends on good intellectual character.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-03.text: Intellectual virtues include humility about your own errors, curiosity, intellectual courage, and fairness to the views of others.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-05.text: The oracle at Delphi said that no one was wiser than Socrates. Socrates tried to refute it by questioning people reputed to be wise.

epistemology-knowledge-30/beat-07.text: A wise knower holds a belief firmly enough to act on it, and loosely enough to revise it.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-00.text: Suppose you’ve left home and wonder whether you locked the door. You can recall locking it.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-01.text: That memory of locking the door is your only evidence.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-02.text: To check, you consult the memory. It seems vivid: the key, the turn, the pull on the handle.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-03.text: Yet a memory’s vividness doesn’t show that it’s accurate.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-04.text: How do you know that this memory is reliable? You recall having checked it before.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-05.text: That recollection is a second memory, so it relies on the same faculty it’s meant to check.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-07.text: A third memory would face the same question. Any check that memory can provide depends on memory itself.

epistemology-knowledge-31/beat-08.text: Only the door itself lies outside memory, so only the door could check the memory independently.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-00.text: Consider four maps of the same stretch of coast, each drawn at a different scale.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-01.text: The first map shows the whole coast as a single line. Nothing on it is false.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-02.text: But it contains almost no information about the coast.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-03.text: The second map shows the coast’s shape and its bays. The third shows every rock.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-04.text: But the third map holds so much detail that it’s too slow to use at sea.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-06.text: The fourth map is drawn at a scale of one to one, with nothing omitted and no errors.

epistemology-knowledge-32/beat-07.text: At that scale, a frame of the same size shows a single rock.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-00.text: Consider a case adapted from Keith DeRose. Asked whether the bank opens on Saturday, you recall being there last Saturday.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-01.text: In ordinary conversation, that memory is enough. You say you know the bank will be open, and nobody objects.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-02.text: Now add high stakes. A cheque must be deposited by Monday, or you’ll lose your house.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-03.text: Your evidence hasn’t changed. The column of evidence is the same height as before.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-04.text: Yet it now seems wrong to say that you know the bank will be open.

epistemology-knowledge-33/beat-07.text: So there is no single height that counts as knowing. On this view, the standard rises as the cost of error rises.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-00.text: Consider two bars. The left bar shows how confident you say you are.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-01.text: The right bar shows how often claims made with that confidence turn out true.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-02.text: At low confidence the two bars agree. When you call something a coin flip, it happens about half the time.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-03.text: The mismatch between the two bars is usually small at this level.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-04.text: Now suppose you say you’re certain. The left bar rises to the top.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-05.text: The right bar doesn’t rise as far. The difference between the bars is overconfidence.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-06.text: Being well calibrated means those two bars match. Calibration is therefore different from being right often.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-07.text: Someone who is right half the time, and claims no more than that, is well calibrated.

epistemology-knowledge-34/beat-10.text: A gap can be closed from either end. Claimed confidence is the end you can change at once.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-00.text: Suppose you see a striped animal in a zoo pen labelled “zebra”. You know at a glance that it’s a zebra.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-02.text: Fred Dretske used this case to test a principle about knowledge.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-03.text: If you know a claim and know that it rules out another, you know that the other is false.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-04.text: The principle is called epistemic closure, because knowledge is closed under known entailment.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-07.text: Yet you never checked whether the animal was a painted mule.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-08.text: The question would strike you as strange, and you’d still say you knew it was a zebra.

epistemology-knowledge-35/beat-09.text: One way out treats the painted mule as an irrelevant alternative. On this view, ordinary looking counts as ruling it out.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-00.text: Consider four pairs of stockings laid out on a counter. All four pairs are identical.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-01.text: Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson asked shoppers which pair was the best quality. Nobody was told the pairs were identical.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-03.text: Asked to explain their choice, the shoppers gave reasons about the stockings themselves.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-04.text: Some said their pair had a better knit. Others pointed to a finer weave.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-05.text: Still others cited sheerness or elasticity, the way a pair felt. However, the four pairs didn’t differ in any of these respects.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-06.text: In fact, the choices were influenced by position in the row. Asked directly, nearly every shopper denied that position had played a part.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-07.text: The denials were sincere. The effect of position was hidden from the shoppers themselves.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-09.text: Each shopper could correctly report which pair seemed best. Nisbett and Wilson grant that people know such judgements.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-10.text: The process behind the choice went unobserved. Introspection, the mind’s view of itself, couldn’t detect it.

epistemology-knowledge-36/beat-11.text: Nisbett and Wilson argue that people infer a likely cause from what’s in front of them. Because the inference goes unnoticed, it feels like memory.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-00.text: Clifford described a shipowner sending an old emigrant ship to sea. The owner had five reasons to doubt she was seaworthy.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-02.text: The owner never had the ship inspected.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-03.text: Instead he suppressed his doubts, one at a time, until they no longer troubled him.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-04.text: The owner watched her leave with a light heart and collected the insurance when she sank. He sincerely believed she was safe.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-06.text: Clifford then altered the case: suppose the ship arrived safely, with the same hull and the same owner.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-07.text: Clifford’s verdict is unchanged, because the owner had no right to believe on that evidence.

epistemology-knowledge-37/beat-09.text: Both are right about different cases. Clifford’s verdict still holds where other people bear the risk of a false belief.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-00.text: Suppose three people are asked the time. All three answer, and two of them are right.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-01.text: Each solid mark shows a person’s belief. The hollow marks show what the same method would have given a minute earlier or later.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-02.text: Two of the beliefs are true. A true belief on its own can’t show whether a reliable method produced it.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-04.text: A belief is called safe when it would still have been true in the most similar nearby cases.

epistemology-knowledge-38/beat-05.text: Bertrand Russell’s example is a stopped clock, read at the one moment it shows the right time. The belief is true, but unsafe.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-00.text: Three judges hear one case. To find the defendant liable, they must agree a contract existed and was broken.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-01.text: Each judge votes on both findings, and each judge’s verdict follows consistently from those two votes.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-02.text: The court’s majority is found by counting each column separately.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-04.text: Lewis Kornhauser and Lawrence Sager named this puzzle the doctrinal paradox. Judges can each be consistent, while the court as a whole is not.

epistemology-knowledge-39/beat-05.text: A court must therefore choose a procedure. It can take a majority on the verdict, or on each premise and let the verdict follow.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-00.text: Does the mind begin empty, or does it contain some knowledge from birth? Empiricists and rationalists give opposing answers.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-01.text: John Locke compared the newborn mind to white paper. All its ideas, he argued, come from sensation or from reflection on its own workings.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-02.text: This view is called empiricism. It holds that the materials of all knowledge come from experience.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-03.text: On Locke’s account, you get the idea of red from seeing red things, and heat from feeling heat. Complex ideas are built by combining such simple ideas.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-05.text: Rationalists reply that some knowledge doesn’t depend on experience. Reason alone can establish certain truths.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-06.text: Descartes and Leibniz held that reason alone can grasp the truths of maths and logic. Knowledge that doesn’t rest on experience is called a priori.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-07.text: In Plato’s Meno, Socrates questions an untaught boy from Meno’s household about how to double a square. Socrates insists he teaches the boy nothing and only asks questions.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-08.text: Plato argues that learning is recollection: the soul already knew these truths before birth.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-10.text: Immanuel Kant argued that each side was partly right. The content of knowledge does come through the senses.

epistemology-knowledge-4/beat-11.text: But the mind orders that content through its own forms, space and time, and concepts such as cause. Knowledge needs both.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-00.text: Suppose a scientific theory makes a prediction, and the prediction fails. Something in the reasoning must be false.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-01.text: In practice, an idea never reaches the evidence on its own.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-02.text: The test also relies on the lens, the calculations, and many unstated assumptions about the setup.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-03.text: So a failed prediction refutes the whole group of assumptions at once. Pierre Duhem made this point in 1906.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-05.text: In the 1840s, Uranus strayed from its predicted orbit. Urbain Le Verrier kept Newton’s law and posited an unseen planet.

epistemology-knowledge-40/beat-07.text: Neptune was found where his calculation predicted. But when the same reasoning was applied to Mercury, it found nothing.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-00.text: Consider a straight oar held up in the air. Here appearance and reality agree: it looks straight and is straight.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-01.text: Now put half of the oar in water. Because light refracts at the surface, the oar looks bent there.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-02.text: The argument from illusion takes three steps. The oar looks bent, but the oar itself is straight.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-03.text: Next, the argument infers that a bent thing is seen. The bent thing can’t be the straight oar, so you see something other than the oar.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-05.text: Bertrand Russell accepted the conclusion. He held that you directly see a sense-datum, a patch of colour and shape, and only infer the oar.

epistemology-knowledge-41/beat-07.text: J. L. Austin rejected the inference. Looking bent in water, he argued, is one of the ways a straight oar looks.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-00.text: Aristotle opens his Metaphysics with a claim about human nature. He writes that “all men by nature desire to know”.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-01.text: On this view, nobody needs to be taught to want knowledge. The desire comes with being human.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-02.text: Aristotle ranks the kinds of knowledge. The highest, wisdom, isn’t valued for its usefulness but is sought for its own sake.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-03.text: Aristotle calls wisdom the only free science. Just as a free person exists for their own sake, so does wisdom.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-04.text: Aristotle offers evidence from ordinary life: people delight in their senses, and above all in sight.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-05.text: People enjoy seeing even when it serves no purpose. Sensation is the lowest rung of Aristotle’s ladder of knowledge.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-06.text: Plato and Aristotle both hold that philosophy begins in wonder. Plato says so in the Theaetetus, Aristotle in the Metaphysics.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-07.text: Aristotle links wonder to perplexity. Someone puzzled by what they can’t explain becomes aware of their own ignorance.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-08.text: Nearly two thousand years later, Francis Bacon gave knowledge a new purpose. For Bacon, knowledge is worth having for the power it gives over nature.

epistemology-knowledge-5/beat-09.text: Aristotle prized understanding nature for its own sake. Bacon prized knowledge that could be used to control nature.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-00.text: Could every belief be doubted? The ancient Pyrrhonian sceptics pressed doubt further than Descartes, who used doubt only as a method.
