epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-01.text: Scepticism asks whether anything can be known. For each reason to believe a claim, the sceptic finds an equal reason against it.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-02.text: Equipollence is a balance of opposing reasons on both sides. Neither belief is then better supported than the other.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-03.text: Pyrrhonian sceptics, named after Pyrrho of Elis, respond by suspending judgement. The Greek term for this suspension is epoche.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-04.text: Sextus Empiricus holds that suspending judgement brings not despair but tranquillity, or ataraxia.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-07.text: However, the claim that nothing can be known refutes itself. To know that claim would be to know something.

epistemology-knowledge-6/beat-08.text: Sextus Empiricus avoids the objection by not asserting it. His sceptical phrases, he says, report only how things seem to him.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-00.text: The sun has risen every morning in recorded history. What justifies the belief that it will rise tomorrow?

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-01.text: You feel confident that it will. David Hume asked what, if anything, justifies that confidence.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-02.text: Induction is inference from observed cases to unobserved ones. For example, every swan seen so far was white, so all swans are white.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-03.text: Everyday expectations and much of science depend on inferences of this kind.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-04.text: Induction assumes that the future will be like the past. The only evidence for this is past experience.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-05.text: But arguing from past experience assumes the very principle in question. Hume concludes that any such justification is circular.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-07.text: Bertrand Russell gives an example. A chicken fed every day comes to expect food, until one day the farmer wrings its neck instead.

epistemology-knowledge-7/beat-08.text: No number of past confirmations can guarantee the next case. The chicken’s evidence was strong, and its conclusion was false.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-00.text: Suppose a friend tells you the bus comes at eight. You ask what reason your friend has for believing it.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-01.text: Your friend gives a reason. You then ask what justifies that reason.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-02.text: Each reason can be questioned in the same way. The question is whether this process must ever stop.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-03.text: Each reason offered is itself a belief. A belief can justify another only if it is justified itself.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-04.text: Each block stands for a belief offered as a reason for the belief above it.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-05.text: The first reason is that the timetable says so. Because a reason supports the belief above it, the chain grows downward.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-06.text: But the belief that the timetable is correct needs justifying too.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-07.text: So a further question arises: why trust the timetable?

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-08.text: The answer is that the city printed it. That raises the question of why the city should be trusted.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-09.text: If every reason needs a further reason, the questions never run out.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-10.text: This is the regress problem, which goes back to Aristotle. If each justification needs another, no belief seems finally justified.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-11.text: The chain of reasons can end in only three ways. First, it may never end, and run on for ever.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-12.text: Second, the chain may loop back in a circle, with beliefs supporting one another. Third, the chain may end in beliefs needing no further support.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-14.text: Foundationalism holds that some beliefs are basic. They need no support from other beliefs, and all other beliefs rest on them.

epistemology-knowledge-8/beat-15.text: On this view, the demand for further reasons finally ends at a basic belief.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-00.text: Truth is something people value. Yet it’s hard to say what makes a belief true.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-01.text: When you call a statement true, what are you claiming about it?

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-02.text: Consider a landscape with two hills and a single tree. The landscape is part of the world outside the mind.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-03.text: The hills and the tree are there whether or not anyone observes them.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-04.text: Now suppose you sketch the landscape: two hills, one tree. The sketch stands for a belief, a claim about the land.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-05.text: The question is what makes such a claim true.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-07.text: Choosing that map applies the classical account of truth. A belief is true when it matches how things are.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-08.text: Truth, on this view, is a relation of fit between a belief and the world. The view is called the correspondence theory.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-10.text: Suppose you try to check a belief against the world. You hold up the sketch and compare it with the land.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-11.text: This raises a difficulty for the correspondence theory: what is the sketch compared against?

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-13.text: The coherence theory gives a different answer. A belief is true if it fits with the rest of what you believe.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-14.text: On this theory, truth is a matter of fitting into the whole web of belief.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-15.text: Pragmatism gives another response. William James held that a true belief is one that works in practice.

epistemology-knowledge-9/beat-16.text: A true map must guide you across the real hills reliably, over time. Being comforting is not enough: the belief must keep working in experience.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-00.text: Suppose you’ve just done something. Afterwards, without anyone asking, a question about the act comes to mind.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-01.text: The question is whether the act was right. It’s a judgement about your own conduct.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-02.text: Other social animals show sympathy and a sense of fairness. Darwin argued that human morality grew from such instincts.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-03.text: Humans add a further capacity, reflection. A person can step back from a deed and ask whether it was right.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-04.text: The answer is given in reasons, weighed for and against the act. No other animal is known to deliberate in this way.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-05.text: That inward weighing is your conscience. It judges your own acts even when no one else can see them.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-06.text: The origin of conscience is disputed. Darwin locates it in instinct, Freud in society turned inward, and Kant in reason itself.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-07.text: Aristotle asked a different question. He asked not which rules to follow, but what makes a human life go well.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-08.text: Aristotle held that reason is the capacity that distinguishes human beings from other living things.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-09.text: So, for Aristotle, living well means exercising reason well, and doing so over a complete life.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-13.text: Aristotle calls the highest human good eudaimonia. It’s often translated as happiness, but it’s an activity, not a feeling.

ethics-ethics-1/beat-14.text: Flourishing is a closer translation. It means living and acting well, from a virtuous character, over a complete life.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-00.text: Suppose you pass a shallow pond, wearing expensive shoes, and see a child drowning. No one else is nearby.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-01.text: Almost everyone judges that you must wade in. The cost of ruined shoes is trivial beside a child’s life.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-02.text: Peter Singer’s argument begins from that shared judgement. It then asks what principle explains the reaction.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-03.text: So you wade in, despite the shoes. Singer then asks an uncomfortable question: did your reason depend on the child being near you?

ethics-ethics-10/beat-05.text: Now suppose another child faces the same danger nine thousand kilometres away, and helping costs you just as little.

ethics-ethics-10/beat-06.text: If distance makes no moral difference, the duty extends to the distant child. The argument helped inspire effective altruism.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-00.text: Suppose every pleasure could be measured in one unit, like coins. Then all your pleasures could be added into a single total.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-01.text: Jeremy Bentham, the founder of modern utilitarianism, treated pleasure this way. Consider three pleasures: a bar game, a dessert and a symphony.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-02.text: For Bentham, pleasures differ only in quantity, so no pleasure is better in itself than another.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-03.text: Bentham’s felicific calculus scores pleasures by how intense, lasting and certain they are. If the pleasure is equal, he held, push-pin is as good as poetry.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-04.text: John Stuart Mill was raised on Bentham’s ideas, yet he rejected this purely quantitative view of pleasure.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-05.text: Mill argued that pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity. Some are higher in kind than others.

ethics-ethics-11/beat-09.text: Once pleasures differ in kind, quantity alone can’t decide which pleasure is better. Mill’s test is the preference of competent judges who have experienced both.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-00.text: Kant proposed a single test for whether an action is permissible. Could you consistently will that everyone act on the same rule?

ethics-ethics-12/beat-01.text: Suppose you need money and promise to repay a loan, knowing you can’t. Kant calls the principle behind such an act its maxim.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-02.text: Kant never asks what the act costs you. He asks whether your rule could be a law that everyone follows.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-03.text: So suppose everyone adopted the maxim of false promising at once.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-05.text: If everyone promised falsely when in need, no one would believe a promise. Promises would become empty words.

ethics-ethics-12/beat-06.text: The maxim therefore contradicts itself. As a universal law, it would destroy the practice of promising it relies on.

ethics-ethics-13/beat-00.text: Theories of rules and of outcomes judge what you do. Aristotle’s virtue ethics judges who you are: your traits of character.

ethics-ethics-13/beat-01.text: Aristotle places courage between two vices. The coward fears too much and flees dangers that should be faced.

ethics-ethics-13/beat-02.text: The rash person is too bold and rushes into dangers that should be avoided. Excess, like deficiency, is a vice.

ethics-ethics-13/beat-04.text: Yet the mean isn’t a fixed halfway point. Aristotle holds that it shifts with the person and the situation.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-00.text: Imagine a condition with no laws, no police and no government. Hobbes and Locke call it the state of nature.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-01.text: In it, you may do whatever you judge necessary, and so may everyone else.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-02.text: Hobbes argues that everyone should leave this condition. The case for leaving is not that freedom is bad.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-03.text: The case is that everyone else has freedom too, and can use it against you.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-04.text: The remedy is the social contract. Each person gives up some liberty, provided everyone else does too, and gains order in return.

ethics-ethics-14/beat-05.text: John Locke adds a right of resistance. People may resist any government going beyond its authority by violating rights.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-00.text: Consider a plain report, the sentence “You stole that money.”

ethics-ethics-15/beat-01.text: The sentence is true or false, and anyone can check it against the world.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-02.text: Now add a moral word: “You acted wrongly in stealing that money.”

ethics-ethics-15/beat-03.text: On a scale that weighs facts, the second sentence weighs no more than the first.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-04.text: Ayer’s emotivism holds that a moral word adds no further fact to the sentence.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-05.text: Instead, the word expresses disapproval. Ayer compares it to saying the sentence in a tone of horror.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-07.text: Moral realists reply that the scale is the wrong instrument. If cruelty is wrong, that’s a fact about cruelty.

ethics-ethics-15/beat-08.text: So a test for observable facts would miss moral facts, if they exist.

ethics-ethics-16/beat-00.text: Suppose a robber holds a knife at your back, and you hand over your wallet. No one would call that act free.

ethics-ethics-16/beat-01.text: A week later, you hand a friend the same money to repay a loan. Both acts are the effects of earlier causes.

ethics-ethics-16/beat-02.text: Hard determinists hold that every event, including every choice, is fixed by earlier causes. So neither act was free.

ethics-ethics-16/beat-04.text: David Hume defends a smaller notion of freedom, compatible with causation. You act freely when you do as you will and nothing forces you.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-00.text: Suppose a murderer comes to your door and asks where your friend is hiding. May you lie to him?

ethics-ethics-17/beat-01.text: Kant answers that you may not. The duty of truthfulness holds even towards a murderer.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-02.text: The verdict seems monstrous. Kant defends it with an argument about consistency, not with revulsion at lying.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-03.text: Kant calls the rule behind an action its maxim. You may act only on a maxim you could will to be a universal law.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-04.text: Kant’s test asks what would follow if everyone adopted your maxim at once. Here, it tests a maxim of lying whenever it suits you.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-05.text: A lie deceives only a listener who expects the truth. If everyone lied, no one would expect the truth, and no lie could deceive.

ethics-ethics-17/beat-08.text: Benjamin Constant objected that a murderer has no right to the truth. No one, he argued, has a right to a truth that harms others.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-00.text: A pig can feel fear and pain, and it would rather avoid both. Does that give the pig moral standing, a claim to moral consideration?

ethics-ethics-18/beat-01.text: Philosophers from Aristotle to Kant tied moral standing to the capacity to reason. Kant held that only rational beings are ends in themselves.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-02.text: Animals can’t argue, make promises or bear duties. So, on this view, they count only as things.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-03.text: However, the rationality test also excludes some human beings. Infants can’t reason.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-04.text: Nor can some people with severe mental disabilities. Yet they still count morally, so reason can’t be the test.

ethics-ethics-18/beat-06.text: Replace reason with Bentham’s criterion: sentience, the capacity to suffer. The boundary of moral concern then includes the pig.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-00.text: Consider four decisions, each about your own life, and who is entitled to make them.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-01.text: Paternalism is interfering with a person’s choices for their own good. Here, the state has decided three of them for you.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-02.text: John Stuart Mill proposed a single test, and it doesn’t concern how risky a choice is.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-03.text: The test asks whether the choice harms anyone other than the person making it.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-05.text: Three rows are signed by the state, and one by you. Mill’s test asks which of these signatures is legitimate.

ethics-ethics-19/beat-07.text: The harm principle is easy to accept while the choices are small. It’s hardest to accept when refusing treatment will end a life.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-00.text: Suppose you find a wallet on the pavement. What should you do with it?

ethics-ethics-2/beat-01.text: Three ethical theories will each deliver a verdict on this one small choice.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-02.text: Moral philosophy offers three main approaches, here called lenses. The first asks what consequences an act will have.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-03.text: The second asks what your duty requires. The third asks what the act makes of your character.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-04.text: Ordinary moral thinking mixes the three. Most people use all three without noticing which one they’re using.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-05.text: John Stuart Mill’s utilitarianism judges acts by consequences. Returning the wallet is right if it produces the most happiness.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-06.text: For Mill, consequences alone determine whether an act is right, and each person’s happiness counts equally.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-08.text: Immanuel Kant sets consequences aside. He holds that you should act only on a rule you could will everyone to follow.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-09.text: Apply Kant’s test to the rule “keep any wallet you find”. Willed for everyone, it would let others keep your lost wallet, so you couldn’t consistently will it.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-10.text: Aristotle’s virtue ethics asks a third question. It asks not what to do, but what character you’re developing.

ethics-ethics-2/beat-11.text: Aristotle holds that virtue is acquired by practice. Each honest act makes the next easier, until honesty is part of your character.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-00.text: Consider seven identical harms. They differ only in when they occur, from now to five hundred years ahead.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-01.text: Governments apply a discount rate, which makes a future cost count for less the later it falls. At typical rates, a harm two centuries away counts for almost nothing.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-02.text: Some discounting has good reasons. A distant benefit is less certain, and future people may be richer than you.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-03.text: Set those reasons aside, and one further discount may remain. Pure time preference counts a harm for less only because it comes later.

ethics-ethics-20/beat-05.text: Without any discount, the seven harms are equal again. Each falls on a person who didn’t choose which century to be born in.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-00.text: A doctor gives enough morphine to stop a patient’s pain. The doctor foresees that the dose will also shorten the patient’s life.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-01.text: One act has two certain effects. The doctor intends only one of them.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-02.text: Thomas Aquinas held that one act can have two effects, one intended and one not. The doctrine of double effect grew from this idea.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-04.text: Now consider a second case with the same two outcomes. Here, the death is the means by which the pain ends.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-05.text: The doctrine judges the second case differently. You may accept a harm alongside your aim.

ethics-ethics-21/beat-06.text: But you may not bring about a harm as the means to your aim.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-00.text: A theory of well-being says what makes a life go well for the person living it. Candidates include pleasure, achievement, being loved, knowing the truth and doing things yourself.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-01.text: Robert Nozick, in 1974, imagined an experience machine. It gives you any experience you want, and while plugged in you believe it’s real.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-02.text: Nozick asks whether you’d plug in for life. He expects most people to refuse, and asks what their refusal shows.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-04.text: The machine is connected to one good only. It supplies pleasure, which is a matter of how your life feels from the inside.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-05.text: The other four goods require facts about the world. The machine can supply only the experience of them.

ethics-ethics-22/beat-07.text: Hedonism holds that pleasure is the only thing good in itself. If it were true, plugging in would be an easy choice, so refusing is evidence against hedonism.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-00.text: Suppose you pass a shallow pond where a small child is drowning. Wading in to save the child would ruin an expensive pair of shoes.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-01.text: Peter Singer holds that you ought to wade in. The ruined shoes are insignificant beside the death of a child.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-02.text: Your obligation to the child at your feet is therefore at its fullest. The verdict seems to need no argument at all.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-03.text: Now suppose a second child, eight thousand miles away, is dying of a preventable disease. You could save this child with the same certainty, at the same small cost.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-05.text: Singer asks what could justify a weaker obligation to the distant child. It can’t be the cost, because the cost is the same.

ethics-ethics-23/beat-06.text: Nor can it be your ability to help, which is also equal. For Singer, the only difference left is distance, and distance is not a moral property.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-00.text: What justifies a four-year sentence? In an ordinary case, four standard answers all support it.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-01.text: Incapacitation protects the public by stopping the offender from offending again. General deterrence discourages others from copying the crime.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-02.text: Rehabilitation aims to make him a better person. Retribution says he should be punished for what he did.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-03.text: Consider a man of ninety, ill and harmless, forty years after his crime. He won’t reoffend, needs no reform, and no one will learn of his punishment.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-04.text: Three of the four justifications no longer apply to him. If his sentence still seems right, some other justification must support it.

ethics-ethics-24/beat-07.text: Critics of deterrence turn the test around. Suppose the truth stays hidden, and framing an innocent man would stop others from crime.

ethics-ethics-25/beat-00.text: Paternalism is interference with a person’s liberty for that person’s own good. When, if ever, is it justified?

ethics-ethics-25/beat-01.text: John Stuart Mill proposed one principle in On Liberty, in 1859. It’s known as the harm principle.

ethics-ethics-25/beat-02.text: On this principle, power over an adult is justified only to prevent harm to others.

ethics-ethics-25/beat-03.text: For Mill, a person’s own good is not a sufficient warrant for compulsion. It justifies persuasion, but never force.

ethics-ethics-25/beat-05.text: Mill tests the principle on a bridge known to be unsafe. A stranger is walking towards the gap, and there’s no time to warn him.

ethics-ethics-25/beat-06.text: Mill says you may seize him and turn him back. This is no real infringement of liberty, because he doesn’t want to fall.

ethics-ethics-25/beat-08.text: Once the stranger is warned, Mill holds, he may decide for himself whether the risk is worth taking. A warning informs his will, whereas force would override it.

ethics-ethics-26/beat-00.text: Kicking a rock wrongs nothing, while kicking an animal seems to wrong the animal. Which beings can be wronged?

ethics-ethics-26/beat-01.text: A being has moral status if it matters morally for its own sake, not merely as a means for others.

ethics-ethics-26/beat-02.text: Three main criteria are defended. They’re the capacity to suffer, the capacity to plan a life, and being human.

ethics-ethics-26/beat-03.text: On the species criterion, only the person stands inside the line. The chimp, the fish, the plant and the rock all fall outside.

ethics-ethics-26/beat-05.text: Being a person and being human are different properties. A person is a being that plans, reflects and knows it has a future.

ethics-ethics-26/beat-07.text: Each criterion puts the line in a different place. Suffering lets in the fish, while planning lets in few beings besides the person.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-00.text: Suppose someone says that cruelty is wrong. Metaethics asks what such a sentence means, and whether it can be true or false.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-01.text: A moral realist takes it to state a fact, true whether or not anyone agrees.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-02.text: A cultural relativist takes it to be true within one culture, with no authority outside it.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-03.text: An expressivist takes it to express a feeling of disapproval, although it has the grammar of a statement.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-05.text: Alfred Ayer defended an early form of this view, emotivism, in 1936. On his view, a moral sentence expresses an attitude and is neither true nor false.

ethics-ethics-27/beat-07.text: Each reading has a cost, which appears when two cultures disagree. Realism must explain what moral facts are, while the other two can’t call either culture mistaken.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-00.text: A principle you accept can approve an act that your gut rejects. That gut reaction is an intuition, a judgement about a particular case.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-01.text: A principle says “always maximise happiness”. A judgement about a case says “framing an innocent man is monstrous”.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-02.text: When the two conflict, consistency requires revising at least one of them. The question is which.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-03.text: John Rawls’s answer is reflective equilibrium. You adjust the principle and the judgement in turn until they fit.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-05.text: Many intuitions once thought obvious proved to be prejudice. Many elegant principles proved too simple for real cases.

ethics-ethics-28/beat-07.text: The goal is coherence between principles and judgements. No belief in the system is a fixed foundation beyond revision.

ethics-ethics-29/beat-00.text: In 1958, James Urmson described a soldier who throws himself onto a grenade to save his squad. Everyone calls the act heroic.

ethics-ethics-29/beat-01.text: A second question is harder. Would the soldier have been blameworthy if he had stayed where he was?

ethics-ethics-29/beat-02.text: Urmson argued that he wouldn’t be, so the act goes beyond duty. A supererogatory act is good and not required.

ethics-ethics-29/beat-03.text: Such an act is praiseworthy if done, and not blameworthy if left undone. The special praise it earns depends on its not being owed.

ethics-ethics-29/beat-05.text: Consider three responses to others’ need. One person gives a fair share, one donates a kidney to a stranger, and one walks past.

ethics-ethics-29/beat-07.text: Common sense praises the kidney donor highly and expects the fair share. Whether walking past deserves blame is less clear.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-00.text: Consider one moral choice, judged by three philosophers.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-01.text: All three seek the right action, yet their verdicts differ.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-02.text: Suppose a runaway trolley is heading towards five people on the track. You stand beside a lever.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-03.text: If you pull it, the trolley switches to a side track, where it will kill one person instead.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-04.text: Three major ethical theories address the case. Each asks the same question: what makes an action good?

ethics-ethics-3/beat-05.text: John Stuart Mill’s utilitarianism says to pull the lever. For Mill, the right act produces the most happiness, counting each person equally.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-06.text: Five lives saved outweigh one lost. Judging acts by outcomes is consequentialism, and Mill’s version is utilitarianism.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-07.text: Immanuel Kant’s ethics rejects the trade. It holds that the one person has a worth no arithmetic can outweigh.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-08.text: This worth is what Kant calls dignity. In deontology, the ethics of duty, a duty binds whatever the consequences.

ethics-ethics-3/beat-09.text: Aristotle shifts the question from the act to the agent. Who does this choice make you?

ethics-ethics-3/beat-10.text: In virtue ethics, the guide is what a practically wise person would do. Aristotle calls this wisdom phronesis.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-00.text: Ethics has three major normative theories. The practical question is how to use all three when making a real decision.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-01.text: Consequentialism judges an act by its outcomes. It asks which available act will bring about the best consequences.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-02.text: Deontology judges an act by whether it respects duties and rights. The deontologist asks what moral rules apply and what each person is owed.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-03.text: Virtue ethics focuses on character. It asks what a virtuous person would do, and which traits the act would build in you.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-05.text: Suppose you learn that a colleague is secretly defrauding customers. You must decide whether to speak or stay silent.

ethics-ethics-30/beat-07.text: Often the three theories give the same verdict. When they conflict, no formula decides between them.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-00.text: Suppose you have a duty to fetch something from a high shelf. The question is whether that duty depends on your ability to reach it.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-01.text: Given a ladder, you climb four rungs. Your reach grows, but the shelf is still some way above you.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-02.text: The duty is unchanged, because the task is still possible for you. Being closer to the shelf doesn’t make the duty any stronger.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-03.text: Then the ladder ends. Even at full stretch you can’t reach the shelf, so the task is now impossible.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-04.text: When a task becomes impossible, the duty to perform it lapses. This principle is called “ought implies can”.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-06.text: Once the ladder is extended, the duty returns at once. Nothing about your character has changed, only your ability.

ethics-ethics-31/beat-07.text: So the duty depends on ability, not on merit. It holds while the task is within your power and lapses when it isn’t.

ethics-ethics-32/beat-00.text: Suppose one person has thought about a hard moral question for years. A second person, who hasn’t thought about it, asks them for the answer.

ethics-ethics-32/beat-01.text: The first person’s verdict rests on reasons: cases weighed, objections answered, earlier views revised. The verdict is only the conclusion of that reasoning.

ethics-ethics-32/beat-02.text: Accepting a moral verdict on someone else’s word is called moral deference. Both people now hold the same true verdict, but only one holds the reasons.

ethics-ethics-32/beat-04.text: Now a new case arises, similar to the first but not identical. Here the difference between the two of them has practical consequences.

ethics-ethics-33/beat-00.text: Suppose you could give part of what you have to people in severe poverty. The question is how much morality requires you to give.

ethics-ethics-33/beat-01.text: Giving some of it helps, and the major ethical theories agree that some giving is required. The dispute concerns how much.

ethics-ethics-33/beat-02.text: Yet after each gift, there’s still another life that a little more could help.

ethics-ethics-33/beat-03.text: So the question is what, if anything, permits you to stop giving.

ethics-ethics-33/beat-04.text: Taken strictly, Peter Singer’s principle says to keep giving until more would cost you as much as it helps others. Singer accepts this.

ethics-ethics-33/beat-07.text: Susan Wolf objects from the opposite direction. She argues that a life devoted wholly to morality is not the best life for a person.

ethics-ethics-33/beat-08.text: In Wolf’s view, such a life crowds out the non-moral interests and talents that make up a rich, well-rounded character.

ethics-ethics-34/beat-00.text: Consider a world of ten people, each with an excellent life. On the total view, how good a world is depends on the sum of wellbeing in it.

ethics-ethics-34/beat-01.text: Now add more people, while making each life somewhat less good.

ethics-ethics-34/beat-02.text: The total still rises, because the added lives more than offset the lost quality.

ethics-ethics-34/beat-03.text: Repeated often enough, the step yields a vast population whose lives are barely worth living. Its total good is greater than in any earlier world.

ethics-ethics-34/beat-04.text: Derek Parfit named the result the Repugnant Conclusion in 1984. He rejected the conclusion, but didn’t succeed in finding a theory that avoids it.

ethics-ethics-34/beat-07.text: An obvious reply is to rank worlds by how good the average life is. This average view has problems of its own.

ethics-ethics-35/beat-00.text: Consider James Rachels’ case of two men and a child in the water. The first man holds the child under until he drowns.

ethics-ethics-35/beat-01.text: The second man sees the child slip under the water and does nothing to save him.

ethics-ethics-35/beat-03.text: Now match the two cases. Both men have the same motive, since each stands to inherit if the child dies.

ethics-ethics-35/beat-04.text: The outcome is the same as well, since the child dies in both cases.

ethics-ethics-35/beat-07.text: Defenders of the distinction reply that real cases are rarely matched like this. Killing and letting die usually differ in other ways too.

ethics-ethics-36/beat-00.text: Suppose someone wrongs you. The wrong leaves three things behind: what happened, whose fault it was, and what you are owed.

ethics-ethics-36/beat-01.text: Now suppose you forgive the person who wronged you.

ethics-ethics-36/beat-02.text: Forgiving leaves the past unchanged. So what does forgiveness change?

ethics-ethics-36/beat-04.text: Forgiving is often confused with excusing. To excuse someone is to judge the person not responsible for the wrong.

ethics-ethics-36/beat-05.text: Forgiving, by contrast, assumes that the person was responsible for the wrong.

ethics-ethics-36/beat-07.text: On Jeffrie Murphy’s account, resentment is a fitting response to a wrong, and you’re entitled to it.

ethics-ethics-36/beat-08.text: Forgiveness is therefore a gift, which only the wronged person may give or withhold.

ethics-ethics-36/beat-10.text: This account doesn’t make forgiveness easy, owed or always right. It explains why only the person wronged can choose to forgive.

ethics-ethics-37/beat-00.text: Consider two people on an ordinary Tuesday. At this point, neither owes the other anything.

ethics-ethics-37/beat-01.text: Now one speaker says four words: “I promise I will.”

ethics-ethics-37/beat-02.text: Those words create an obligation that binds the speaker to the other person.

ethics-ethics-37/beat-03.text: David Hume found this puzzling. Nothing else changes: no money moves and no law is passed.

ethics-ethics-37/beat-04.text: Yet a duty now exists where none existed a moment before. Hume concluded that only a human convention could explain the change.

ethics-ethics-37/beat-06.text: Meanwhile, the other person has come to rely on the promise, and has cancelled a plan.

ethics-ethics-37/beat-07.text: They’ve told a friend and stopped looking for any other arrangement.

ethics-ethics-37/beat-10.text: A secret breach separates the two accounts. If the wrong were only to the practice, a breach that no one discovers would leave the practice almost untouched.

ethics-ethics-38/beat-00.text: Suppose two children are drowning and you can save only one. One of them is your own child.

ethics-ethics-38/beat-01.text: Impartial moral theories set aside whose child is whose. Each life counts equally, whoever it belongs to.

ethics-ethics-38/beat-02.text: The question is which reasons for favouring one child an impartial rule can accept.

ethics-ethics-38/beat-04.text: William Godwin accepted the strictest version. Faced with a fire, he said, save Archbishop Fénelon rather than his maid, even if she is your mother.

ethics-ethics-38/beat-05.text: Bernard Williams replies that the tie itself is a reason. A parent who saves their own child needs no impartial permission.

ethics-ethics-39/beat-00.text: Suppose it’s midnight and you judge that you should sleep. You start another episode anyway.

ethics-ethics-39/beat-01.text: Acting on your better judgement involves three steps: judging which option is better, intending to take it, and acting.

ethics-ethics-39/beat-03.text: On this picture, the weak-willed person judges and intends, but stops before acting. Socrates denied that anyone ever stops there.

ethics-ethics-39/beat-04.text: In Plato’s Protagoras, Socrates holds that choosing an act means judging it best at that moment. So a worse choice is an error of judgement, not a failure of will.

ethics-ethics-39/beat-05.text: Aristotle disagreed. He holds that the weak-willed person has the knowledge but isn’t using it, like someone asleep or drunk.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-00.text: Cultures disagree about right and wrong. That disagreement is an observable fact.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-01.text: The claim that no correct answer lies behind the disagreement is much stronger, and logically separate.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-02.text: The first claim is descriptive relativism: societies in fact hold different moral codes.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-03.text: The second claim is moral relativism. It holds that rightness depends on a group’s code, with no higher standard.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-04.text: Inferring the second from the first is a common error. Disagreement doesn’t show there’s no answer.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-05.text: The anthropologist Ruth Benedict defended relativism. For Benedict, a society calls good whatever it has come to approve.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-07.text: Moral objectivists reply that some moral truths hold regardless of culture. Torturing a child for fun is wrong everywhere.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-08.text: Cultures differing does not make every code equally true. Disagreement about the Earth’s shape didn’t make every answer true.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-09.text: Donald Brown looked at cultures all over the world. He found things that every one of them shared, which he called human universals.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-10.text: Human universals include returning a favour, and forbidding murder and incest.

ethics-ethics-4/beat-11.text: These universals suggest a shared moral foundation beneath the differences between cultures.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-00.text: Suppose you promised a dying friend that you’d burn his letters. No one else heard the promise.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-01.text: The promise still stands a month later, but the person you made it to has died.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-02.text: If you break the promise, it’s hard to say who’s worse off as a result.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-03.text: A wrong usually has a victim who can feel its effects. Epicurus held that the dead feel nothing and so can’t be harmed.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-05.text: Joel Feinberg calls such a wish a surviving interest. An interest is a stake in how things go, not a feeling.

ethics-ethics-40/beat-07.text: So an interest can be set back by events its owner never lives to see.

ethics-ethics-41/beat-00.text: Suppose you join a scheme because joining is the default. No one forced you, and no one gave you a reason.

ethics-ethics-41/beat-01.text: There are three broad ways to influence a choice. Two are familiar: persuasion and force.

ethics-ethics-41/beat-02.text: Persuasion offers reasons for the chooser to weigh. Force removes an option altogether.

ethics-ethics-41/beat-03.text: The third leaves every option open but sets the default, the outcome you get by doing nothing. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein call this a nudge.

ethics-ethics-41/beat-05.text: Where organ donation is the default, far more people consent to be donors than where they must opt in.

ethics-ethics-41/beat-07.text: Declining takes the same few seconds in either system. Only the default has changed, yet the outcomes differ widely.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-00.text: In Greece, India and China, thinkers began to argue systematically about how people should live.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-01.text: Karl Jaspers named this period the Axial Age. He argued that these regions, without contact, began asking similar questions.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-02.text: Scholars dispute why this happened, and some doubt that there was a single Axial Age at all.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-03.text: Socrates wrote nothing. His views are known mainly through the dialogues of his student Plato.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-04.text: Socrates questioned Athenians about what virtue is. In 399 BCE, Athens executed him for impiety and corrupting the young.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-05.text: In India, a central concept was dharma. It includes the duties that belong to your place in life.

ethics-ethics-5/beat-06.text: In China, Confucius taught ren, usually translated as humaneness. He held that ren is cultivated in relationships with others.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-00.text: Some acts that save five lives at the cost of one still strike most people as wrong.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-01.text: The numbers can stay fixed while moral intuitions reverse. What changes is how the harm is brought about.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-02.text: Pulling a lever diverts the trolley to kill one instead of five. Later variants change only how the one dies.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-03.text: In Judith Jarvis Thomson’s 1976 footbridge case, you stand on a bridge beside a large stranger. Pushing him onto the track would stop the trolley.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-04.text: In surveys, most people who would pull the lever judge pushing impermissible.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-05.text: Both cases trade one life for five, which is all a utilitarian counts. Yet people judge them differently.

ethics-ethics-6/beat-06.text: The doctrine of double effect offers an explanation. Diverting kills as a side effect, whereas shoving uses a person as a means.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-00.text: Suppose two drivers each look at a phone for two seconds. One drives home safely and forgets the moment.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-01.text: The other soon stands trial in court. Both made the same two-second choice.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-02.text: The first driver’s road is empty, with nothing in the way.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-03.text: The first driver looks away and back, and the road is still clear. She never thinks about it again.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-04.text: The second driver makes the same choice, on a similar road, for the same two seconds.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-05.text: The only difference lies outside the driver’s control: a child is already stepping into the road.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-06.text: At the moment of choice, the two drivers are identical in speed, attention and disregard for risk.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-07.text: Nothing inside the drivers is different at all. Only their circumstances on the road differ.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-09.text: Now consider the outcomes, which luck decides. On road B, the car strikes the child.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-10.text: The second driver faces trial for causing a death. The first goes home, never learning what might have happened.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-12.text: In 1976 Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel called this moral luck: judgement that depends on factors beyond one’s control.

ethics-ethics-7/beat-13.text: Nagel stated the principle of control that such judgements seem to violate.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-00.text: Suppose a friend has been withdrawn for two weeks. You could work out impartially what you owe them.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-01.text: Or you could go and sit with them. Care ethicists argue that moral theory long neglected the second response.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-02.text: Most major theories begin from impartiality. They seek a rule or a welfare total that applies to everyone equally.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-03.text: Their categories apply to anyone and name no particular person.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-04.text: Now suppose a person is on the floor beside their bed. No general category fits their situation.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-05.text: To you, this person isn’t a case or a number. This is someone with whom you have a relationship.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-06.text: You cross the room and kneel beside them. You haven’t yet consulted any theory.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-07.text: Something other than a principle is already guiding what you do.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-09.text: Carol Gilligan studied people who reasoned through relationships and care. Kohlberg’s influential scale ranked such reasoning as less mature.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-10.text: Gilligan called this a different moral voice, centred on responsibility and relationships.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-13.text: Nel Noddings developed a full ethics of care. Its basis is the relation between the one caring and the cared-for.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-14.text: Noddings holds that ethical caring grows from natural caring, such as a parent’s care for a child.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-15.text: Claudia Card warned that care ethics could make a virtue of women’s oppression. Gilligan held that care and justice work together.

ethics-ethics-8/beat-16.text: Justice requires treating everyone equally. Care notices the person the rules never mention.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-00.text: Most hard choices have a right answer, even when it’s difficult to find. A genuine moral dilemma is different.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-01.text: In a genuine dilemma, you ought to do each of two things. You can’t do both.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-02.text: During the German occupation, a student asked Sartre for advice. His elder brother had been killed in 1940, and he wanted to join the Free French.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-03.text: The student’s mother, however, lived only for him, and his departure would plunge her into despair.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-04.text: Neither claim overrides the other, so this is a genuine dilemma. No common scale can weigh one claim against the other.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-06.text: Suppose the student joins the Free French. Suppose, too, that his choice is justified.

ethics-ethics-9/beat-07.text: The claim to stay with his mother remains. Acting on the other claim did not cancel it.

logic-arguments-1/beat-00.text: Consider two people who disagree and who treat their disagreement as a fight.

logic-arguments-1/beat-01.text: What could settle a disagreement is what each side claims and why. The volume of their voices settles nothing.

logic-arguments-1/beat-02.text: Shouting a denial back isn’t a counter-argument. It denies the claim without offering any reason against it.

logic-arguments-1/beat-03.text: After three exchanges, the two have traded insults. Neither has given a reason.

logic-arguments-1/beat-04.text: In everyday speech, the word “argument” often means a shouting match.

logic-arguments-1/beat-05.text: Such an exchange is a quarrel. Because a quarrel contains no reasons, nothing in it can settle the disagreement.

logic-arguments-1/beat-06.text: In philosophy, the word “argument” has a technical meaning. An argument is a set of claims with a definite structure.

logic-arguments-1/beat-07.text: Some of the claims, called premises, are offered as reasons. The claim these reasons support is the conclusion.

logic-arguments-1/beat-09.text: In the fourth century BCE, Aristotle gave the first account of deductive argument.

logic-arguments-1/beat-10.text: In a syllogism, two premises fix the conclusion, so accepting them means accepting it too.

logic-arguments-1/beat-12.text: The loudness of a claim has no bearing on whether it’s true. Only reasons and evidence bear on that.

logic-arguments-1/beat-14.text: Arthur Schopenhauer distinguished two aims a person can have in arguing.

logic-arguments-1/beat-15.text: One aim is to establish the truth, and the other is to win. Schopenhauer listed thirty-eight stratagems for winning, whether or not you’re in the right.

logic-arguments-1/beat-16.text: Socrates argued to test claims rather than to win. At his trial in 399 BCE, he cross-examined his accuser Meletus with questions.

logic-arguments-1/beat-17.text: Meletus said that every Athenian improves the young except Socrates. Socrates showed the claim was absurd by asking whether the same holds for horses.

logic-arguments-1/beat-18.text: Now suppose the same two people take up the same disagreement again, this time with reasons.

logic-arguments-1/beat-19.text: The first speaker now offers a premise: rents have risen while wages haven’t. It’s a factual claim, so it can be checked.

logic-arguments-1/beat-20.text: The second speaker replies that rents fell where more housing was built. That reply challenges the reasoning, not the person.

logic-arguments-1/beat-21.text: The people and the disagreement are unchanged. Because each side now gives reasons, the exchange can make progress.

logic-arguments-1/beat-22.text: John Stuart Mill argued further that you understand your own view only once you understand the opposing one.

logic-arguments-10/beat-00.text: Suppose a friend says “he’s rich, so he must be happy”. The argument states a premise and a conclusion, but it relies on a third claim.

logic-arguments-10/beat-01.text: Being rich and being happy are different conditions. So the argument needs a premise linking them, and that premise is never stated.

logic-arguments-10/beat-02.text: An argument that depends on an unstated premise is called an enthymeme.

logic-arguments-10/beat-03.text: To assess such an argument, its unstated premise has to be made explicit.

logic-arguments-10/beat-05.text: Stated explicitly, the missing premise reads: all rich people are happy.

logic-arguments-10/beat-06.text: Once stated, the premise can be assessed, and it’s false: many rich people are unhappy.

logic-arguments-11/beat-00.text: A proof must rest on support from outside itself. This proof loses that support, although no single step is invalid.

logic-arguments-11/beat-01.text: The proof begins with two premises: this book is God’s word, and whatever God says is true.

logic-arguments-11/beat-02.text: So far, each premise is asserted on its own, and neither is used to support the other.

logic-arguments-11/beat-03.text: Step three answers an obvious objection with “God exists, because the book says so”. Step four concludes that the book is true, and the proof appears to rest on evidence.

logic-arguments-11/beat-05.text: Tested step by step, the proof is valid because each step follows from the one before it.

logic-arguments-11/beat-06.text: That validity is what makes the flaw hard to detect.

logic-arguments-12/beat-00.text: Suppose someone says “you’re either with us or against us”. The sentence offers two options and asks you to choose one.

logic-arguments-12/beat-01.text: Both options are genuine, since some people are with you and some are against you.

logic-arguments-12/beat-02.text: The fallacy lies in the unargued claim that no other option exists. This is called a false dilemma.

logic-arguments-12/beat-03.text: A false dilemma presents the options on offer as if they were all the options.

logic-arguments-12/beat-05.text: Other options existed before the offer was made. Presenting only two hides the rest without eliminating them.

logic-arguments-13/beat-00.text: Consider a modest proposal: one student may retake one quiz. On its own, the proposal is uncontroversial.

logic-arguments-13/beat-01.text: A slippery-slope argument claims that this step will set off a chain of worse ones. First, students will demand to retake every test.

logic-arguments-13/beat-02.text: Next, grades will lose their meaning. So, the argument concludes, no retakes at all should be allowed.

logic-arguments-13/beat-03.text: Each step in the chain is a claim. Between the steps there should be reasons, and this argument gives none.

logic-arguments-13/beat-05.text: A slope argument is legitimate when each step has evidence. Alcohol slows reactions, and slower reactions raise crash risk.

logic-arguments-14/beat-00.text: Consider two premises: nothing is better than eternal happiness, and a ham sandwich is better than nothing.

logic-arguments-14/beat-01.text: Each premise, read on its own, seems true.

logic-arguments-14/beat-02.text: They appear to yield the conclusion that a ham sandwich is better than eternal happiness. The form looks valid, yet the conclusion is absurd.

logic-arguments-14/beat-03.text: The fault is easy to miss, because the form looks valid. So the error must lie in the words, not in the form.

logic-arguments-14/beat-06.text: In the first premise, the word “nothing” means that no thing is better. In the second, it means having nothing at all.

logic-arguments-14/beat-07.text: Because the word “nothing” shifts meaning, the premises share no common term. This fallacy is called equivocation.

logic-arguments-15/beat-00.text: Suppose two tourists were rude to you last week, and both came from the same country.

logic-arguments-15/beat-01.text: In this case, both observations are true.

logic-arguments-15/beat-02.text: You conclude that people from the country are rude. This hasty generalisation draws a claim about a nation from two people.

logic-arguments-15/beat-03.text: Firsthand evidence feels compelling because you witnessed it. Yet two cases, however vivid, don’t establish a pattern.

logic-arguments-15/beat-05.text: A sample supports a general conclusion when it’s large enough and fairly chosen. A sample of two people met by chance is neither.

logic-arguments-16/beat-00.text: Suppose that every morning a cockerel crows, and a few minutes later the sun rises.

logic-arguments-16/beat-01.text: Over five mornings the order never varies: first the crow, then the sunrise.

logic-arguments-16/beat-02.text: The inference would be that the crowing makes the sun rise. Here, no one accepts that conclusion.

logic-arguments-16/beat-03.text: Yet the same form of inference is common where the conclusion seems plausible.

logic-arguments-16/beat-04.text: The fallacy is called post hoc ergo propter hoc. In Latin that means “after this, therefore because of this”.

logic-arguments-16/beat-05.text: Every cause comes before its effect, but so does every coincidence.

logic-arguments-16/beat-07.text: On the sixth morning the cockerel is ill and silent. The sun rises at the usual time.

logic-arguments-17/beat-00.text: Suppose a man you know to be dishonest tells you, in two different ways, that the bridge will hold.

logic-arguments-17/beat-01.text: The left claim comes with its reasons, the steel’s rating and two load tests. It’s an argument.

logic-arguments-17/beat-02.text: The right claim rests on nothing but the speaker’s word, which makes it testimony.

logic-arguments-17/beat-03.text: Suppose you reply by attacking the man: he lies, so no one should listen to him.

logic-arguments-17/beat-04.text: The reply feels decisive, but it addresses only the speaker.

logic-arguments-17/beat-05.text: Only the reasons escape the insult, which lands equally on both columns.

logic-arguments-17/beat-08.text: An argument can be assessed by examining its reasons. Testimony falls with the speaker, because nothing else supports it.

logic-arguments-18/beat-00.text: Suppose one person tells you the town’s water is safe to drink, and you know nothing else about it.

logic-arguments-18/beat-01.text: Now suppose the whole town says the same thing, and some residents are angry with you for doubting it.

logic-arguments-18/beat-02.text: In this machine, the handle stands for the number of believers and the strength of their feeling. The needle shows whether the claim is true.

logic-arguments-18/beat-03.text: Treating popularity as evidence is the bandwagon fallacy. Treating strong feeling as evidence is the appeal to emotion.

logic-arguments-18/beat-04.text: The shaft between them is broken. Popularity and feeling have no bearing on whether a claim is true.

logic-arguments-18/beat-06.text: Evidence, unlike popularity, is connected to the truth of a claim. A test of the water bears on whether it’s safe.

logic-arguments-19/beat-00.text: Four cards each have a letter on the front and a number on the back. The rule says a vowel on the front means an even number on the back.

logic-arguments-19/beat-01.text: Which cards must be turned over to test the rule? In Peter Wason’s selection task, the most common answer is the vowel and the even number.

logic-arguments-19/beat-02.text: Turning the four can’t refute the rule. A vowel on its front would satisfy the rule, and the rule says nothing about consonants.

logic-arguments-19/beat-04.text: The seven has a vowel on its front. One counterexample is enough to show that the rule is false.

logic-arguments-19/beat-05.text: Wason explained the common answer by confirmation bias, the tendency to seek cases that confirm a belief. Only a card that could refute the rule can test it.

logic-arguments-2/beat-00.text: In logic, an argument is a set of claims, some of which are offered as reasons for another.

logic-arguments-2/beat-01.text: Every argument, however long, is built from the same basic parts. Once you can identify them, you can analyse any argument.

logic-arguments-2/beat-02.text: Two stones form a base, and a third rests on top. The top stone stands only because the two below support it.

logic-arguments-2/beat-03.text: This shape is the basic form of an argument: claims below that support a claim above.

logic-arguments-2/beat-04.text: The stones at the base are the premises, the reasons offered for a claim. The words “because” and “since” often introduce a premise.

logic-arguments-2/beat-05.text: The stone on top is the conclusion, the claim the premises support. In a deduction, Aristotle held, the conclusion follows of necessity.

logic-arguments-2/beat-06.text: The words “therefore”, “so” and “thus” often introduce a conclusion.

logic-arguments-2/beat-08.text: This is the standard example of a syllogism, the form of argument Aristotle first analysed.

logic-arguments-2/beat-09.text: If both premises are true, the conclusion can’t be false. That’s what Aristotle meant by a conclusion that follows of necessity.

logic-arguments-2/beat-11.text: Remove the premises and nothing supports the conclusion. The premises are what give anyone a reason to accept it.

logic-arguments-20/beat-00.text: Consider three reports of the claim “screens are making us worse at paying attention”. None of them is a lie, and none adds anything false.

logic-arguments-20/beat-01.text: The reports differ only in how many of the supporting reasons they repeat. One repeats all of them.

logic-arguments-20/beat-02.text: A second repeats some of them. The third repeats a single reason.

logic-arguments-20/beat-03.text: A straw man is not usually a lie. It’s an objection to the weakest version of a view, presented as an objection to the view itself.

logic-arguments-20/beat-05.text: The weakest version falls, but the stronger versions remain. So the claim itself is still unrefuted.

logic-arguments-20/beat-06.text: The remedy is called steelmanning. It means building the strongest form of the other side’s view and answering that form instead.

logic-arguments-21/beat-00.text: Consider four conditions that might bear on whether a fire starts. Each relates to the fire in a different way.

logic-arguments-21/beat-01.text: Necessity and sufficiency are separate questions. A condition is necessary when removing it stops the fire from starting.

logic-arguments-21/beat-02.text: A condition is sufficient when it starts the fire alone.

logic-arguments-21/beat-03.text: A match in petrol starts a fire every time, so it’s sufficient. It isn’t necessary, because a spark could start the same fire.

logic-arguments-21/beat-05.text: It being Tuesday is neither necessary nor sufficient. Fuel, heat and oxygen together are both necessary and sufficient.

logic-arguments-21/beat-06.text: So there are four kinds of condition. A common mistake is to take a sufficient one for a necessary one, or the reverse.

logic-arguments-22/beat-00.text: For centuries, Europeans accepted the claim “all swans are white”. In 1697, Dutch sailors saw black swans in Western Australia, and the claim was refuted.

logic-arguments-22/beat-01.text: Aristotle sorted claims about groups into four forms: all, none, some, and some-not. The universal claim “all cats are black” covers every cat in the group underneath.

logic-arguments-22/beat-02.text: A universal claim asserts something of every member of a group. Such a claim says a great deal, but one exception makes it false.

logic-arguments-22/beat-04.text: One cat isn’t black, so the claim “all cats are black” is false. The seventeen black cats can’t restore it.

logic-arguments-23/beat-00.text: Propositional logic uses four basic connectives: and, or, not, and if. Each builds a compound claim from simpler ones.

logic-arguments-23/beat-01.text: Take two claims, P and Q, each either true or false. A truth table lists all four combinations, one per row.

logic-arguments-23/beat-02.text: In everyday speech, the word “or” often means one but not both. In logic, the claim “P or Q” is true when at least one part is true.

logic-arguments-23/beat-03.text: So the claim “it will rain or snow” is true on a day with both. This is called inclusive disjunction.

logic-arguments-23/beat-05.text: The claim “if P, then Q” is called a conditional. It says that whenever P is true, Q is true as well.

logic-arguments-23/beat-06.text: A conditional is false in only one case: when P is true and Q is false.

logic-arguments-23/beat-08.text: When P is false, the conditional isn’t falsified. So the material conditional of classical logic counts it as true.

logic-arguments-24/beat-00.text: Sherlock Holmes calls his method deduction. Most of his conclusions are in fact inferences to the best explanation.

logic-arguments-24/beat-01.text: Deduction moves from premises to a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true.

logic-arguments-24/beat-02.text: Induction moves from many observed cases to a general rule that’s probably true, but not certain.

logic-arguments-24/beat-03.text: Abduction moves from an observation to the hypothesis that would best explain it.

logic-arguments-24/beat-05.text: A deduction’s conclusion already sits inside the premises that feed it. The inference just states what they say.

logic-arguments-24/beat-07.text: Deduction’s certainty has a cost. The conclusion adds no fact that the premises did not already give.

logic-arguments-25/beat-00.text: Suppose a test that’s ninety-nine per cent accurate gives you a positive result for a disease. It seems to follow that you’re almost certainly ill.

logic-arguments-25/beat-01.text: That inference can be badly wrong, because it ignores how rare the disease is.

logic-arguments-25/beat-02.text: The disease affects one person in ten thousand, which is its base rate. Suppose ten thousand people are tested.

logic-arguments-25/beat-03.text: One of the ten thousand is ill, and the test almost certainly detects that person. That gives one true positive.

logic-arguments-25/beat-05.text: However, the test also wrongly flags one per cent of the healthy people. That’s about a hundred false positives, or false alarms.

logic-arguments-26/beat-00.text: Proof by contradiction, or reductio ad absurdum, proves a claim indirectly. Begin by assuming it is false.

logic-arguments-26/beat-01.text: Then reason validly, one careful step at a time, from that assumption until a contradiction appears.

logic-arguments-26/beat-02.text: Suppose there’s a largest whole number. Call it N.

logic-arguments-26/beat-03.text: Supposing a claim doesn’t assert it. Any claim may be assumed for the sake of argument.

logic-arguments-26/beat-04.text: N plus one is also a whole number, and it’s larger than N.

logic-arguments-26/beat-05.text: So N is not the largest after all, which contradicts the original assumption.

logic-arguments-26/beat-07.text: Valid steps can’t lead from true premises to a contradiction. Every later step was valid and used only true facts, so the assumption must be false.

logic-arguments-26/beat-08.text: So the assumption is false, and there’s no largest whole number.

logic-arguments-27/beat-00.text: Consider the sentence “this sentence is false”. Is the sentence true, or is it false?

logic-arguments-27/beat-01.text: Suppose the sentence is true. Then what it says is the case, so it’s false.

logic-arguments-27/beat-02.text: Suppose instead that the sentence is false. Then what it says isn’t the case, so the sentence is true.

logic-arguments-27/beat-03.text: The source of the trouble is self-reference. An ordinary sentence describes the world, but this one describes itself.

logic-arguments-27/beat-05.text: This is the liar paradox, often credited to Eubulides of Miletus. Epimenides, a Cretan, said that his own people always lie, though the claim can be false without contradiction.

logic-arguments-27/beat-07.text: Bertrand Russell found a similar paradox in set theory. Kurt Gödel used self-reference to prove his incompleteness theorems.

logic-arguments-28/beat-00.text: An argument by analogy rests on one claim: two cases are alike, so they should be treated alike.

logic-arguments-28/beat-01.text: An argument by analogy is inductive. Its conclusion is never certain, and the argument is only as strong as the likeness it rests on.

logic-arguments-28/beat-02.text: An analogy is strong when the cases share features relevant to the conclusion. It’s weak when the shared features are superficial.

logic-arguments-28/beat-03.text: A single relevant difference can defeat the whole argument. Such a difference is called a disanalogy.

logic-arguments-28/beat-05.text: Judith Jarvis Thomson builds an analogy about abortion. She likens a pregnancy from rape to being tied to a violinist who needs your body to live.

logic-arguments-28/beat-07.text: Suppose someone argues that banning hate speech is justified because falsely shouting fire in a theatre is banned.

logic-arguments-29/beat-00.text: Suppose someone claims that a china teapot orbits the sun between Earth and Mars, too small to be seen.

logic-arguments-29/beat-01.text: No one could disprove the claim, and Bertrand Russell chose the example for that reason. Yet being impossible to disprove gives no reason to believe a claim.

logic-arguments-29/beat-02.text: The burden of proof is the obligation to support a claim with evidence. It falls on whoever asserts.

logic-arguments-29/beat-03.text: Before any evidence is offered, the default is to withhold belief. Withholding belief is neither acceptance nor denial.

logic-arguments-29/beat-05.text: Carl Sagan describes someone who says an invisible dragon lives in their garage. Each test for the dragon is explained away.

logic-arguments-29/beat-07.text: Sagan argues that a dragon no test can detect is no different from no dragon at all.

logic-arguments-3/beat-00.text: An argument can have a flawless logical form and still reach a false conclusion, if its premises are false.

logic-arguments-3/beat-01.text: Logic distinguishes two tests. An argument is valid when its form makes it impossible for true premises to yield a false conclusion.

logic-arguments-3/beat-02.text: An argument is sound when it’s valid and all its premises are true.

logic-arguments-3/beat-03.text: Consider an argument whose premises are that all toasters are gold and all gold things are time machines.

logic-arguments-3/beat-04.text: Its conclusion is that all toasters are time machines. If the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true, so the argument is valid.

logic-arguments-3/beat-05.text: Both premises are false, and so is the conclusion. Valid form, false premises: the argument is valid but not sound.

logic-arguments-3/beat-08.text: Validity concerns only the form, while soundness also concerns the truth of the premises. To reject the conclusion of a valid argument, you must reject a premise.

logic-arguments-30/beat-00.text: This unit has analysed arguments by taking them apart. The same tools can be used to build one.

logic-arguments-30/beat-01.text: Begin with the conclusion you mean to defend. Then find premises that, if true, would guarantee it.

logic-arguments-30/beat-02.text: Next, make every hidden assumption explicit. A premise left unstated can’t be checked, and it may be false.

logic-arguments-30/beat-03.text: Check that the argument is valid, then check whether each premise is true. A valid argument with true premises is called sound.

logic-arguments-30/beat-05.text: Once the argument is built, test it yourself. Identify its weakest premise and the objection a critic would raise.

logic-arguments-30/beat-07.text: Construct the strongest version of each objection and answer that. This practice is called steelmanning.

logic-arguments-31/beat-00.text: Suppose a fair coin is flipped again and again. On every flip, heads and tails are equally likely.

logic-arguments-31/beat-01.text: The coin lands heads three times in a row. The probability of three heads in three flips is one in eight.

logic-arguments-31/beat-02.text: The chance of heads on the next flip is still one half. The three earlier heads leave it unchanged.

logic-arguments-31/beat-03.text: After seven heads, tails feels overdue. The gambler’s fallacy is the belief that a run makes the opposite outcome more likely.

logic-arguments-31/beat-04.text: Yet the chance of heads on the eighth flip is still one half.

logic-arguments-31/beat-06.text: In 1913, a roulette wheel at Monte Carlo landed on black twenty-six times in a row. Gamblers lost heavily by betting that red was overdue.

logic-arguments-31/beat-07.text: Each spin was independent. The outcome of one spin doesn’t change the chance of any other.

logic-arguments-32/beat-00.text: One person puts a question to another. Whichever way the second person answers, the answer admits a charge.

logic-arguments-32/beat-01.text: The question is “have you stopped cheating at cards?” It appears to be an ordinary yes-or-no question, but it isn’t one.

logic-arguments-32/beat-02.text: If you answer yes, you say you’ve stopped, and so admit that you cheated before.

logic-arguments-32/beat-03.text: The accusation is now on the record, although no one ever stated it.

logic-arguments-32/beat-04.text: Answering no seems safer, but it’s worse. It means you haven’t stopped, which admits that the offence continues.

logic-arguments-32/beat-05.text: A question like this is called a loaded question: it presupposes a claim that any direct answer concedes.

logic-arguments-33/beat-00.text: Consider seven measurements plotted on a graph, with a straight line drawn through them. The line is simple, but it misses most of the points.

logic-arguments-33/beat-01.text: A moderately curved line fits much better. It passes near every point and still describes a general pattern.

logic-arguments-33/beat-02.text: Add enough bends, and a curve can pass through every point. Its fit to the seven measurements is perfect.

logic-arguments-33/beat-03.text: No measurement is left unexplained, so this curve seems to be the best available account of the data.

logic-arguments-33/beat-04.text: However, an eighth measurement falls far from the perfect curve. A curve can fit past data and still fail to predict new data.

logic-arguments-33/beat-05.text: The curve had fitted the errors in the seven measurements along with the pattern. This failure is called overfitting.

logic-arguments-33/beat-08.text: Occam’s razor is named after William of Ockham. It says to prefer the account with fewer parts when two fit the evidence equally well.

logic-arguments-33/beat-09.text: Every extra part is another assumption that could be false, and another way to fit measurement error.

logic-arguments-34/beat-00.text: Suppose a jar holds marbles, and you want to know what fraction of them are dark. The true fraction is fixed, but finding it would mean counting every marble.

logic-arguments-34/beat-01.text: You draw a handful at random and estimate the fraction from that sample. The band around the estimate marks how far it might be from the true value.

logic-arguments-34/beat-02.text: A sample this small can give an estimate far from the true fraction.

logic-arguments-34/beat-03.text: As the sample grows, the band narrows quickly at first. Each marble drawn is evidence about the others left in the jar.

logic-arguments-34/beat-04.text: However, the gains soon diminish. It takes four times the sample to halve the width of the band.

logic-arguments-34/beat-05.text: Sampling error depends on the square root of the sample size, not on the size itself. So each gain in precision costs more than the last.

logic-arguments-34/beat-08.text: Now consider a large sample drawn only from people who answered the phone. The sample is biased if those people differ from everyone else.

logic-arguments-34/beat-09.text: The error band is narrow, but it’s centred on the wrong value. The estimate is precise without being accurate.

logic-arguments-35/beat-00.text: Consider two quantities, each recorded every week over one summer.

logic-arguments-35/beat-01.text: Ice cream sales rise, and drownings rise with them, week by week. The two quantities are correlated.

logic-arguments-35/beat-02.text: The correlation is real, and it holds too consistently to be a coincidence.

logic-arguments-35/beat-03.text: The arrow reads the correlation as causation. It claims that ice cream sales cause drownings.

logic-arguments-35/beat-04.text: No one believes this causal claim, but the correlation alone can’t refute it. The same data fit more than one causal explanation.

logic-arguments-35/beat-06.text: A common cause of two correlated quantities is called a confounder. Once summer heat is held fixed, the link between ice cream and drowning disappears.

logic-arguments-35/beat-07.text: The correlation was real, but a causal link between the two never existed.

logic-arguments-35/beat-09.text: Confounders are rarely this obvious. Children with bigger feet read better, but only because older children have both.

logic-arguments-35/beat-10.text: Coffee was long linked with a higher risk of death, because coffee drinkers were more likely to smoke.

logic-arguments-36/beat-00.text: Suppose someone claims there’s an elephant in a room. The room is divided into squares, so the extent of a search can be measured.

logic-arguments-36/beat-02.text: An argument from absence concludes that something isn’t there because a search found nothing. Its strength depends on the search’s chance of finding the thing, had it been there.

logic-arguments-36/beat-03.text: Suppose you search two squares of a forest for one beetle. The empty result is almost no evidence of absence, because the forest is large and the beetle small.

logic-arguments-36/beat-06.text: The saying “absence of evidence is not evidence of absence” is therefore only partly true. It applies only to a search that would probably have missed the thing.

logic-arguments-36/beat-07.text: Applied to a thorough search, the saying dismisses a genuine result. So whenever someone uses it, ask how thorough the search was.

logic-arguments-37/beat-00.text: Suppose a village has one barber, who follows one rule. He shaves all and only the men of the village who don’t shave themselves.

logic-arguments-37/beat-01.text: For every other man, the rule gives a clear verdict. A man who shaves himself isn’t shaved by the barber.

logic-arguments-37/beat-02.text: A man who doesn’t shave himself is shaved by the barber.

logic-arguments-37/beat-04.text: The barber shaves himself if and only if he doesn’t, which is a contradiction. A description can be well formed and still describe nothing that could exist.

logic-arguments-37/beat-05.text: In 1901, Bertrand Russell found a contradiction of the same form in the theory of sets. Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves.

logic-arguments-37/beat-06.text: If the set contains itself, it violates its own condition for membership. If the set doesn’t contain itself, it meets the condition and must be included.

logic-arguments-37/beat-09.text: In 1902, the second volume of Frege’s Basic Laws of Arithmetic was in press. Frege added an appendix acknowledging the contradiction, and the volume appeared in 1903.

logic-arguments-38/beat-00.text: An argument has a form that can be separated from its subject matter. The form shown has three steps, and a subject is supplied at the top.

logic-arguments-38/beat-01.text: Anselm of Canterbury defines God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived. He holds that to exist in reality is greater than to exist only in the mind.

logic-arguments-38/beat-02.text: Gaunilo, a monk of Marmoutiers, kept the same three steps and changed only the subject. He applied them to the greatest conceivable island.

logic-arguments-38/beat-04.text: The two arguments share every step and differ only in their subject. So they must both succeed or both fail.

logic-arguments-38/beat-05.text: Any flaw in the island argument’s steps is also in Anselm’s. An argument whose form yields absurd conclusions is said to prove too much.

logic-arguments-39/beat-00.text: Most claims can be refuted only with outside evidence. A few can be refuted by applying them to themselves.

logic-arguments-39/beat-01.text: Consider three claims, each on its own plank. The test is whether each claim meets the standard it sets.

logic-arguments-39/beat-03.text: The claim “nothing can be proved” is itself a claim, so it falls within its own scope. The claim must therefore meet its own demand for proof.

logic-arguments-39/beat-04.text: If the claim is proved, then something can be proved, so the claim is false. If it isn’t proved, it has no support.

logic-arguments-39/beat-05.text: Either way, the claim can’t be defended, and no outside evidence was needed. Such a claim is called self-refuting.

logic-arguments-4/beat-00.text: Some arguments aim to guarantee a conclusion. Others aim only to make the conclusion probable.

logic-arguments-4/beat-01.text: Both kinds of argument are legitimate, and each has its own standard of assessment.

logic-arguments-4/beat-02.text: A deductive argument aims to guarantee its conclusion. It’s judged valid or invalid, and a valid one with true premises is sound.

logic-arguments-4/beat-03.text: An inductive argument aims only to make its conclusion likely, so it’s judged strong or weak. A strong one with true premises is cogent.

logic-arguments-4/beat-04.text: Consider the argument “all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, so Socrates is mortal”. If both premises are true, the conclusion can’t be false.

logic-arguments-4/beat-05.text: That certainty comes from the argument’s form, not from its subject matter.

logic-arguments-4/beat-06.text: Now consider the argument “most Greeks eat olives, Socrates is Greek, so he eats olives”. The premises could be true and the conclusion false.

logic-arguments-4/beat-07.text: So the conclusion is only probable. Judging such an argument by the standard of validity is a mistake.

logic-arguments-40/beat-00.text: Consider a simple case of induction: every emerald checked so far has been green.

logic-arguments-40/beat-01.text: Each observation supports the claim that every emerald is green.
