logic-arguments-40/beat-02.text: Nelson Goodman defined a new predicate, grue. A stone is grue if it’s checked before tonight and is green, or not checked before tonight and is blue.

logic-arguments-40/beat-03.text: Every stone checked so far was checked before tonight and was green. So every stone on record is grue as well.

logic-arguments-40/beat-05.text: The two rules conflict about a stone first checked tomorrow. The green rule predicts green, and the grue rule predicts blue.

logic-arguments-40/beat-07.text: Green seems the simpler predicate. However, simplicity depends on which predicates a language takes as basic.

logic-arguments-41/beat-00.text: Consider Linda, who’s thirty-one, single and outspoken. As a student, she studied philosophy and cared about social justice.

logic-arguments-41/beat-01.text: Is it more probable that Linda is a bank teller, or a bank teller who’s also an activist?

logic-arguments-41/beat-02.text: Most people choose the second, because the added detail matches Linda’s description.

logic-arguments-41/beat-03.text: However, every activist bank teller is a bank teller. So the second group is a subset of the first.

logic-arguments-41/beat-05.text: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman named this error the conjunction fallacy in 1983. Most people they tested made the error, even students trained in statistics.

logic-arguments-41/beat-07.text: Adding a detail narrows a claim, so the claim fits the same cases or fewer. Detail can make a story more convincing while never making it more probable.

logic-arguments-5/beat-00.text: A proof is a sequence of steps that leads from premises to a conclusion. If any single step fails, the proof fails.

logic-arguments-5/beat-01.text: The premises are the claims granted at the start. Each step from claims already granted to a new claim is called an inference.

logic-arguments-5/beat-02.text: An inference is valid when the premises, if true, guarantee that the conclusion is true.

logic-arguments-5/beat-03.text: In Euclid’s first proposition, circles centred on point A and point B meet at point C. Line AC and line BC each equal line AB, so they equal each other.

logic-arguments-5/beat-04.text: The triangle on line AB therefore has three equal sides. Euclid builds this result from a short sequence of stated steps.

logic-arguments-5/beat-07.text: Stating every inference shows where a proof could fail. Descartes’s third rule is to begin with the simplest objects and rise, step by step, to the more complex.

logic-arguments-6/beat-00.text: Many arguments depend on a sentence built with the words “if” and “then”. Logicians call such a sentence a conditional.

logic-arguments-6/beat-01.text: A conditional is a sentence of the form “if P, then Q”. The condition P, introduced by the word “if”, is called the antecedent.

logic-arguments-6/beat-02.text: The result Q, introduced by the word “then”, is called the consequent. The conditional claims a link between the two, not that either is true.

logic-arguments-6/beat-03.text: Consider the sentence “if it rains, the streets get wet”. The sentence asserts neither rain nor wet streets.

logic-arguments-6/beat-04.text: Like a promise, the conditional is broken only if it rains and the streets stay dry. On a day without rain, the promise is kept.

logic-arguments-7/beat-00.text: Two basic forms of inference start from a conditional. Both are valid: true premises guarantee a true conclusion.

logic-arguments-7/beat-01.text: Suppose you accept the rule “if it rains, the streets get wet”. This conditional is the first premise.

logic-arguments-7/beat-02.text: The rule claims only that rain, whenever it falls, makes the streets wet. The rule alone says nothing about today’s weather.

logic-arguments-7/beat-03.text: Now add a second premise, which states a fact: it’s raining.

logic-arguments-7/beat-04.text: The question is what, if anything, these two premises together allow you to conclude.

logic-arguments-7/beat-06.text: This move has a name: modus ponens. Given the rule and its first part, called the antecedent, you may infer its second part, called the consequent.

logic-arguments-7/beat-07.text: The conclusion about the streets follows from the premises alone, without anyone observing the streets.

logic-arguments-7/beat-08.text: Now keep the same rule and take a different second premise, about the streets rather than the sky.

logic-arguments-7/beat-09.text: The second premise is now that the streets are dry.

logic-arguments-7/beat-11.text: The second form is called modus tollens. From a conditional and a false consequent, you may infer a false antecedent.

logic-arguments-7/beat-12.text: A fact about the streets, together with the rule, settles a question about the sky.

logic-arguments-8/beat-00.text: Suppose you’re walking home at night and find a stretch of street soaking wet.

logic-arguments-8/beat-01.text: At once, you conclude that it must have rained.

logic-arguments-8/beat-02.text: Your reasoning relies on a rule you accept: if it rains, the streets get wet.

logic-arguments-8/beat-03.text: Your second premise is that the streets are wet.

logic-arguments-8/beat-04.text: From the premises you infer the antecedent: the streets are wet, so rain fell.

logic-arguments-8/beat-05.text: The inference resembles modus ponens, but runs from the consequent back to the antecedent.

logic-arguments-8/beat-07.text: A little further on, a garden sprinkler has been watering the pavement all evening.

logic-arguments-8/beat-08.text: The sprinkler alone could have made the street wet, whether or not it rained.

logic-arguments-8/beat-09.text: This fallacy is called affirming the consequent. It treats a wet street, the consequent, as proof of rain, the antecedent.

logic-arguments-8/beat-10.text: The inference fails whenever something other than rain could leave the street wet.

logic-arguments-8/beat-11.text: Now consider a second inference, which begins from the absence of rain. Suppose it doesn’t rain tomorrow, and you expect dry streets.

logic-arguments-8/beat-13.text: This fallacy is called denying the antecedent. Without one cause, an effect can still occur through another.

logic-arguments-9/beat-00.text: Suppose someone presents the claim that a budget adds up. A fallacy of distraction seems to rebut a claim while leaving the claim untouched.

logic-arguments-9/beat-01.text: The first is the ad hominem, which attacks the arguer instead of the argument. One such reply says “he failed maths, so ignore his budget”.

logic-arguments-9/beat-02.text: However, a claim’s truth doesn’t depend on who asserts it. The insult says nothing about whether the figures add up.

logic-arguments-9/beat-03.text: The second is the straw man. It replaces the real position with a weaker one nobody holds, and refutes that instead.

logic-arguments-9/beat-04.text: In effect, you defeat a position you built yourself, not your opponent’s.

logic-arguments-9/beat-05.text: Neither reply has engaged with the claim itself. The question of whether the budget adds up is still open.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-00.text: Why is there something rather than nothing? The question asks about everything that exists, taken as a whole.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-01.text: Gottfried Leibniz, in 1714, called it the first question anyone has a right to ask.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-02.text: Leibniz’s principle of sufficient reason says that nothing is true without a reason. Applied to the whole world, it asks why the world exists at all.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-03.text: Leibniz argued that nothing is simpler and easier than something. So a universe that exists, rather than none, needs a reason.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-05.text: Parmenides, an early Greek philosopher, held that what is not cannot be thought or spoken of.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-06.text: Suppose you remove every object, along with space and time. Even the dark void you then picture is still something, because thinking of nothing turns it into a thing.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-07.text: Science explains each state of the universe by an earlier state, together with the laws of nature.

metaphysics-being-1/beat-08.text: So every scientific explanation presupposes that states and laws already exist. It can’t explain why they exist at all.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-00.text: A rose, a ruby and a flag differ in almost every respect. Yet all three share one feature: they are red.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-01.text: Philosophers call a feature that many things share a universal. What, then, is redness, and where does it exist?

metaphysics-being-10/beat-02.text: Treat the shared feature as a single item, redness. This is the problem of universals: how one thing can be in many.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-03.text: The competing theories differ over where such an item exists, if it exists at all.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-04.text: On Plato’s theory, redness would be a Form, existing apart from every red thing. The perfect Red would exist even if nothing were red.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-05.text: Aristotle held that universals are real, but exist only in the particular things that have them.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-06.text: On this view, if no red objects existed, redness wouldn’t exist either.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-08.text: Nominalists deny that there are universals. For them, “red” is a word applied to things that resemble each other.

metaphysics-being-10/beat-09.text: On this view, there’s no further item called redness, in the red things or above them.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-00.text: Over a lifetime, much of the matter in a human body is replaced. Yet the person is still counted as the same person.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-01.text: What, then, makes someone the same person over time?

metaphysics-being-11/beat-02.text: John Locke describes a case involving two people, a prince and a cobbler.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-03.text: The prince’s consciousness reaches back over his past life. He remembers his actions, back to his childhood.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-04.text: Suppose the prince’s consciousness, with all its memories, enters the cobbler’s body overnight. Neither body has moved.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-05.text: The case pulls apart two things that usually stay together: having the same body, and having the same memory.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-09.text: Locke concludes that the man with the prince’s memories is now the prince. The name follows the memories, not the body.

metaphysics-being-11/beat-10.text: Locke distinguishes the same man, one continuing living body, from the same person, one continuing consciousness.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-00.text: Introspection means attending to your own mind. It finds a stream of experiences, such as a warmth, a sound or a passing thought.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-01.text: The question is whether a self exists apart from this stream, as the one who has the experiences.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-02.text: René Descartes holds that a single thinking thing has the experiences. Even when doubting everything else, Descartes can’t doubt his own existence.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-03.text: On this view, the self is a thinking substance that persists while its particular thoughts come and go.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-04.text: David Hume searched his own mind for a self. Each time, Hume found only a particular perception, never a self that has it.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-05.text: Hume concluded that a self is nothing but a bundle of perceptions. The place for an owner stays empty.

metaphysics-being-12/beat-07.text: Buddhist philosophy denies a permanent self in its doctrine of anatta, or not-self. It’s tempting to conclude that, without an owner, there’s no self of any kind.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-00.text: Suppose a scanner records every cell of your body, destroys the original, and builds an exact replica on Mars. Would you step in?

metaphysics-being-13/beat-01.text: Suppose it works. The replica is psychologically continuous with you, linked to your past by your memories and intentions.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-02.text: Now suppose the scanner fails to destroy the original. You walk out of the machine on Earth.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-03.text: The replica walks out on Mars with your memories and intentions. Both of you continue the mental life of the person who stepped in.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-05.text: Psychologically, the two have an equal claim to be you. The one on Earth also keeps your original body.

metaphysics-being-13/beat-06.text: Identity can’t branch, because one person can’t be identical to two different people. Psychological continuity, however, has branched.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-00.text: Consider four claims, each true in the actual world. Beside them are five possible worlds, consistent ways things could have been.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-01.text: Each claim is marked in every world where it’s true. Two of the claims are true in all five worlds.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-02.text: The other two claims are true in some worlds and false in others.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-03.text: A claim true in every possible world is a necessary truth. It could not have been false.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-04.text: A claim true in only some worlds is a contingent truth. It’s true, but it might have been false.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-06.text: The two necessary truths differ in how they can be known. One is a priori, knowable by reason alone.

metaphysics-being-14/beat-07.text: The other is a posteriori, known only through watching and testing.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-00.text: Consider one ball striking another, which then rolls away. The first ball seems to make the second one move.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-01.text: David Hume asks what observation reveals when one event causes another.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-02.text: You observe the first ball moving, and then its contact with the second ball.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-03.text: Then the second ball moves. You see contact and one event after another, but you never see the necessary connection.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-04.text: A necessary connection is a link that makes the effect follow. If such a link can be observed, it must lie between contact and motion.

metaphysics-being-15/beat-06.text: Hume finds the two events conjoined but never observed to be connected. So the idea of connection can’t come from the objects.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-00.text: Harry Frankfurt describes two addicts with the same craving, the same dose and the same physical dependence.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-01.text: The two addicts differ only in their attitude to the craving. The willing addict endorses his desire for the drug.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-02.text: The unwilling addict hates his craving, yet it still moves him to take the drug.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-03.text: Frankfurt calls a desire about a desire a second-order desire. A first-order desire is a desire to do something, such as take the drug.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-04.text: Frankfurt’s central notion is a second-order volition, wanting a particular desire to be the one that moves you.

metaphysics-being-16/beat-06.text: Freedom of the will, on this account, doesn’t depend on a desire’s origin. It depends on something beyond the desire itself, whether the agent endorses it.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-00.text: Frank Jackson imagines Mary, a scientist who knows every physical fact about colour vision, down to which neurons fire.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-01.text: By the terms of the case, her physical knowledge of colour is complete.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-02.text: However, Mary has never seen colour. She’s lived her whole life in a black and white room.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-03.text: Suppose she leaves the room and sees a red rose. Jackson argues that she learns something she didn’t know before.

metaphysics-being-17/beat-05.text: David Chalmers classes explaining how the brain processes light among the easy problems. Explaining why any of it is felt is the hard problem.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-00.text: Consider four things, three of which have a location you can point to.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-01.text: The apple, the chair and the star each occupy a place in space and time. Each is a concrete object.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-02.text: The number three has no such place. It isn’t a group of three apples.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-03.text: Nor is it the numeral chalked on a board, which is only a sign for the number.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-04.text: Yet claims about three are true. Three is a prime number, and it was prime before anyone counted.

metaphysics-being-18/beat-06.text: Platonism, after Plato, gives the obvious answer. On this view, numbers exist as abstract objects outside space and time.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-00.text: Consider an apple and all of its properties. The apple is red, round and sweet, weighs eighty grams, and sits on this table.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-01.text: Remove one property, its colour, and something is still there to have the rest.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-02.text: Now remove the shape, the taste, the weight and the location as well.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-03.text: Once every property is gone, either something remains or nothing does. Substance theory and bundle theory give opposite answers.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-04.text: John Locke held that a substance underlies the properties and holds the properties together. Yet Locke admitted that such a substance is unknown.

metaphysics-being-19/beat-07.text: The bundle theory faces a hard case. Suppose a second apple has every property on the first apple’s list.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-00.text: A thing is contingent if it could have failed to exist. The universe appears to be contingent.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-01.text: This raises the question why there is something rather than nothing. No answer to it is generally accepted.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-02.text: Gottfried Leibniz’s principle of sufficient reason holds that nothing is without a reason.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-03.text: The principle then applies to existence itself. There must be a reason why anything exists at all.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-04.text: Leibniz held that nothing is simpler and easier than something. So existence, not nothingness, is what requires a reason.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-05.text: Parmenides, more than two thousand years before Leibniz, asked whether there could be nothing at all.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-06.text: In his poem On Nature, a goddess sets out two ways of inquiry. One says “it is”, and the other says “it is not”.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-08.text: The goddess calls the second way wholly unlearnable. There’s nothing on it to find or follow.

metaphysics-being-2/beat-09.text: What is not cannot be walked on, pointed at, or thought about. It is not a genuine alternative to what is.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-00.text: Begin with a single world, which is real. The simulation argument doesn’t deny that this world exists.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-01.text: Nick Bostrom asks you to suppose that a civilisation like ours learns to run a world on a computer.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-02.text: Such an advanced civilisation might run many thousands of simulations of its own past history.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-03.text: Simulated minds would then vastly outnumber unsimulated ones. Yet each simulated mind would take its world to be real.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-04.text: Suppose nothing you know tells you whether your own mind is simulated.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-05.text: By Bostrom’s principle of indifference, your mind is then most likely a simulated one.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-08.text: Two of the three possibilities imply that few such simulations are ever run. Civilisations may die out first, or may choose not to run them.

metaphysics-being-20/beat-09.text: In either case, the number of simulated minds falls.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-00.text: Represent time as a line, with you standing at the present moment. The question is not whether time passes.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-01.text: It asks which parts of the line exist: the past, the present, the future, or only some of them.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-02.text: Presentism says only this instant exists. Past things aren’t stored in some other region of time.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-03.text: On this view, yesterday doesn’t exist anywhere. It existed once, and no longer exists at all.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-04.text: C. D. Broad’s growing block theory holds that the past and present exist, but the future doesn’t exist yet. As time passes, new moments are added.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-06.text: Eternalism holds that every moment exists. On this view, the word “now” works like the word “here”: it marks only the speaker’s position in time.

metaphysics-being-21/beat-08.text: Einstein’s theory makes it hard to say presentism is true. Two people moving at different speeds do not agree on which events are happening now.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-00.text: Suppose you must choose between speaking up and staying quiet. Represent the choice as a railway junction with two branches.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-01.text: Now imagine the moment replayed, with the same past and the same laws of nature.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-02.text: Determinism holds that the past and the laws of nature fix a single future. So every replay takes the same branch.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-03.text: Hard determinism accepts this and adds that freedom requires a real alternative. So no one is free, and no one deserves blame.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-05.text: Compatibilism holds that the phrase “could have done otherwise” means you’d have acted differently had you wanted to. On this reading, determinism leaves freedom intact.

metaphysics-being-22/beat-07.text: Libertarianism about free will holds that a choice could go either way on an exact replay. The luck objection replies that nothing about you then settles which branch is taken.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-00.text: Consider a ship kept in service for centuries. Whenever a plank rots, it’s removed and replaced with a new one.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-01.text: Eventually no original plank remains. The ship keeps the same name, berth and crew, but none of the original wood.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-02.text: Thomas Hobbes extended the puzzle. Suppose someone kept every discarded plank and reassembled them into a second ship.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-04.text: Two tests of sameness, which normally agree, come apart here. Continuous use favours the repaired ship.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-05.text: Sameness of material favours the reassembled ship. No further fact about the ships decides between the two tests.

metaphysics-being-23/beat-07.text: The puzzle rests on a deeper question, the special composition question. When do many parts compose one object?

metaphysics-being-23/beat-08.text: A pile of planks is not a ship, although it contains the same material.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-00.text: Consider a heap of sand, and remove a single grain.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-01.text: What remains is still a heap, which seems obvious. A single grain seems too small to make a difference.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-02.text: The case supports a general premise: removing one grain from a heap always leaves a heap. Each later step applies only this premise.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-03.text: Apply the premise repeatedly. After half the grains are gone, the pile still counts as a heap, because no single removal changed the verdict.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-05.text: Applied down to the last grain, the premise says a single grain is a heap. Every step seems valid and the premise seems true, yet the conclusion is false.

metaphysics-being-24/beat-06.text: This is the sorites paradox, named after the Greek word for heap. One of the assumptions must be given up, and philosophers disagree about which.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-00.text: Suppose you almost missed your train this morning. What makes the claim that you could have missed it true?

metaphysics-being-25/beat-01.text: Represent your life up to this morning as a single road.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-02.text: This morning the road forks, one branch for each way events could have gone. A complete way things could have been is called a possible world.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-03.text: The road you took represents the actual world. The other roads represent worlds that are merely possible.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-05.text: A claim is necessary if it’s true in every possible world, and possible if it’s true in at least one.

metaphysics-being-25/beat-06.text: David Lewis asked what possible worlds are. Do the other roads exist as fully as the actual one?

metaphysics-being-25/beat-08.text: Lewis intended this as a literal claim. On his modal realism, other worlds are as concrete as the actual world and contain counterparts of you.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-00.text: Hydrogen is flammable and oxygen supports burning, yet together they form water, which puts out fires.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-01.text: Neither gas is wet, yet water is. Wetness is a property of the whole that neither part has.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-02.text: Consider a simpler case, a traffic jam. No single car is a jam, yet the cars together make one.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-03.text: Each driver brakes in response to the car ahead. Yet the jam as a whole moves backwards along the road at its own speed.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-05.text: Weak emergence is surprising behaviour that still follows from the parts. A traffic jam is weakly emergent.

metaphysics-being-26/beat-07.text: Strong emergence claims more: some features of a whole can’t be derived, even in principle, from its parts.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-00.text: Gravity has never failed. Yet never failing is different from having to hold.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-01.text: Consider two bags of marbles. Every marble in both bags is blue.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-02.text: In the second bag, a machine paints each marble blue before it enters. In the first, every marble is blue by accident.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-03.text: David Hume found no necessary connection between events. For him, a law is only a pattern that always holds.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-05.text: David Armstrong held that a law is a link of necessitation between properties, such as heat and volume.

metaphysics-being-27/beat-07.text: Dispositional essentialism puts the necessity inside things. Mass attracts because attracting is part of what mass is.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-00.text: Where does consciousness come from? The usual answer is that matter becomes conscious once it’s organised enough.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-01.text: Panpsychism disagrees. It holds that some simple form of experience exists at the most basic level of nature.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-02.text: Panpsychists don’t claim that rocks think. They claim that fundamental particles have the simplest form of experience.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-03.text: Physics describes what matter does, not what matter is in itself. Panpsychists propose that its intrinsic nature is experience.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-05.text: Leibniz called the simplest substances monads. Each has its own perceptions and is closed to outside influence.

metaphysics-being-28/beat-07.text: Emergentism answers instead that experience appears only once matter reaches a certain level of organisation.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-00.text: Consider a tree falling where no one perceives it. Does the tree still exist when no mind perceives it?

metaphysics-being-29/beat-01.text: Realism holds that the world exists and has its nature independently of minds. Unobserved mountains would still exist.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-02.text: Anti-realism holds that what’s real depends on minds. For the idealist, to exist is to be perceived.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-03.text: George Berkeley argued that an unperceived tree can’t even be conceived. Anyone imagining one is perceiving it in thought.

metaphysics-being-29/beat-05.text: James Boswell records that in 1763 Samuel Johnson kicked a large stone and declared, “I refute it thus.”

metaphysics-being-29/beat-07.text: Now suppose every conscious being ceased to exist at once, leaving no mind anywhere.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-00.text: Plato holds that an apple in your hand is only partly real. It lies between what fully is and what is not.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-01.text: Heraclitus held that all things flow, like a river you can’t step into twice. Plato accepted this of perceptible things.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-02.text: Knowledge needs an object that doesn’t change, so Plato divided reality in two. Being is unchanging, and it can be known.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-03.text: Becoming is always changing, so it’s grasped only by opinion, through the senses.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-04.text: In Plato’s allegory of the cave, prisoners chained since childhood take shadows for reality. One is freed and forced up into daylight, where he sees the things themselves.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-05.text: Plato holds that the cave is the world of the senses. The things outside it, lit by the sun, stand for the Forms.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-07.text: Every physical thing is an imperfect copy of a Form. Equal sticks fall short of the Form of Equal, which is never unequal.

metaphysics-being-3/beat-08.text: So knowledge is possible only of the unchanging Forms. Of changing things, there can be only opinion.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-00.text: Metaphysicians have debated the same questions for two and a half thousand years. Has any of them been answered?

metaphysics-being-30/beat-01.text: The critic’s charge is that science settles questions and moves on, while metaphysics still debates claims raised in antiquity.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-02.text: Defenders reply that progress here isn’t a matter of settled questions. It means sharper questions and fewer defensible answers.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-03.text: Consider an analogy: a cave explored in darkness. Each expedition charts new passages and records the dead ends.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-05.text: Travellers who come later start from your map rather than from nothing.

metaphysics-being-30/beat-07.text: Physics takes time, cause, law and possibility for granted. Working out what these really are is not a job for experiments.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-00.text: Consider a solid slab of cheese. Everything in it is a material thing, cheese all the way through.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-01.text: Suppose three holes are made in it. Nothing was added to the cheese, and some was removed.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-02.text: Yet a count now finds three more things than before, the three holes.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-03.text: Holes can be counted and measured, and one hole can be deeper than another.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-04.text: Talk about holes therefore seems to commit you to the existence of holes.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-06.text: What, then, was counted? There are three candidates.

metaphysics-being-31/beat-07.text: The cheese, the ring of cheese around each gap, or the empty gap itself.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-00.text: Consider a universe containing two iron spheres and nothing else: no stars, no observers, no ground.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-01.text: Max Black’s case, from 1952, tests Leibniz’s identity of indiscernibles: things sharing every property are identical.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-02.text: The two spheres are alike in every way: same size, same material, same age, and same warmth. They have always existed together.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-03.text: Their relational properties match too. Each is two miles from a sphere qualitatively identical to it.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-04.text: Every description you write of one is a true description of the other.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-06.text: You could call one of them sphere A. But naming requires an observer, and this universe contains none.

metaphysics-being-32/beat-07.text: Remove the label and nothing in the universe changes, because the label was never part of it.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-00.text: Consider a tower of nine blocks. A single still frame doesn’t show which way time runs.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-01.text: Now the tower falls. Everyone has watched towers fall, and the event seems to need no explanation.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-02.text: Now reverse the film. A scattered heap of blocks assembles itself into a standing tower.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-03.text: Anyone can tell at once that the reversed film shows something that doesn’t happen.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-04.text: Yet every collision in the reversed film obeys the laws of physics. This is the puzzle of time’s arrow.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-05.text: The basic laws of motion are time-symmetric: any collision run in reverse is also permitted by them.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-08.text: This is Ludwig Boltzmann’s explanation of entropy increase. Ordered arrangements are rare, and disordered ones are common.

metaphysics-being-33/beat-09.text: A system moving at random therefore drifts into disorder and almost never returns to order.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-00.text: Consider an ordinary table, whose existence no one doubts.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-01.text: Even so, metaphysics asks what the table’s existence depends on.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-02.text: The question isn’t what caused the table or who owns it. It asks what the table’s existence rests on.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-03.text: The answer isn’t the legs. What makes the object a table is something else.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-04.text: The table exists because its wood is arranged in a certain way. Philosophers call this relation grounding.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-05.text: Grounding isn’t causation: the wood doesn’t come before the table. It lies underneath, at a more basic level.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-06.text: Asked of the wood, the question leads to molecules and atoms. The word atom means uncuttable in Greek.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-09.text: A level that rests on nothing is what fundamental means. This differs from being smallest or earliest.

metaphysics-being-34/beat-10.text: Fundamentality is about which things depend on which.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-00.text: Represent your life as a line through time. You stand at the present end.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-01.text: Now suppose you travel back to 1925. So far, the idea of visiting the past involves no contradiction.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-02.text: Being present in 1925 need not change any event that happened there.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-03.text: Suppose that in 1925 you shoot your grandfather before he meets your grandmother. Then you’re never born.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-04.text: But then no one travels back to fire the shot, so you’re born after all. This is the grandfather paradox.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-08.text: One response keeps history consistent. If you were always in 1925, whatever you did there is part of what happened.

metaphysics-being-35/beat-09.text: Your attempt fails for an ordinary reason, such as a jammed gun. In the only consistent history, it never succeeded.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-00.text: Consider a hotel with infinitely many rooms, all occupied. A new guest arrives and asks for a room.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-02.text: The proof for one guest is simple. The guest in room one moves to room two, the guest in room two to room three, and so on.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-03.text: Every guest still has a room, and room one is now empty.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-04.text: The move works only because there’s no last room. In a hotel of a hundred rooms, the guest in room one hundred would have nowhere to go.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-07.text: The mathematics is consistent. Only an endless collection can be paired one to one with a proper part of itself.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-08.text: William Lane Craig argues that such a hotel shows an actual infinite can’t exist in reality.

metaphysics-being-36/beat-09.text: Whether any real collection behaves this way is a separate question from whether the mathematics is consistent.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-00.text: Consider a glass that stood on a shelf for ninety years. It was never knocked or dropped, and it never broke.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-01.text: Was the glass fragile? Almost everyone would say yes, but it’s hard to say what that claim is about.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-03.text: The simple conditional analysis defines fragility plainly: strike the object, and the object breaks.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-04.text: Now suppose a hammer comes down on the glass.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-05.text: But a sorcerer stands ready to toughen the glass the moment a blow begins. So the glass doesn’t break.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-06.text: Yet until the blow, the glass is as fragile as ever. So the simple conditional analysis fails.

metaphysics-being-37/beat-09.text: Dispositions are therefore unusual facts. The glass’s fragility is real now, yet it concerns a breaking that never occurs.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-00.text: Consider one piece of clay on a potter’s bench over three days.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-01.text: On Monday the clay is a lump, and on Tuesday it’s shaped into a vase. On Wednesday the potter squashes it back into a lump.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-02.text: So the clay existed for three days, but the vase existed for only one.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-04.text: Yet they still differ in how long they last. Things that differ in any way can’t be one and the same.

metaphysics-being-38/beat-05.text: Saul Kripke argued that identity is necessary. If two names refer to one thing, they couldn’t have referred to two.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-00.text: Suppose a plant dies because no one waters it. The cause appears to be an absence, an omission.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-01.text: Consider four people who could have watered it. None of them did so all week.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-02.text: For each person, ask what would have happened had they watered it. In every case, the plant would have lived.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-04.text: The counterfactual test counts the gardener as a cause, but it counts the king and the stranger too.

metaphysics-being-39/beat-05.text: The test comes from David Hume. One thing causes another if, without the first, the second wouldn’t have happened.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-00.text: To say “nothing exists” is already to speak about something. Parmenides identified this problem in the fifth century BCE.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-01.text: Suppose you try to think of nothing. It becomes the object of your thought, and a thought must be about something.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-02.text: Each attempt to refer to nothing turns it into something, such as the object of a thought.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-03.text: Parmenides of Elea described two ways of inquiry. One holds that it is, and the other that it is not.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-04.text: Parmenides rejects the second way, because what is not can be neither known nor said. So only what is can be real.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-06.text: This conclusion rules out change. To change, a thing would have to pass into or out of not-being, which Parmenides has excluded.

metaphysics-being-4/beat-07.text: So motion itself is false, a mere show put on by the senses. Aristotle later replied that “being” is said in more than one way, including potential and actual being.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-00.text: Tomorrow it will either rain or not rain. That either-or statement, called a disjunction, seems beyond doubt.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-01.text: Classical logic accepts the principle of bivalence. It holds that every statement is either true or false.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-02.text: Applied to tomorrow, bivalence implies that one of the two predictions is already true today.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-03.text: In Aristotle’s example, a sea battle is predicted for tomorrow. If the prediction is true today, the battle seems bound to happen.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-05.text: On the traditional reading, Aristotle denies bivalence for future contingents, claims about what may or may not happen. Such a claim is neither true nor false yet.

metaphysics-being-40/beat-07.text: A second reply, defended by William of Ockham, keeps bivalence. It accepts that a prediction can be true now, but denies that truth makes the event necessary.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-00.text: Suppose the whole universe were shifted three feet east. Everything in it would move together, by the same distance.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-01.text: Newton held that space is absolute. Space exists in its own right, whether or not anything occupies it.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-02.text: Leibniz held that space is relational: nothing but the order among coexisting things. Without things, there would be no space.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-03.text: The two views therefore disagree about the shifted universe. On Newton’s view it’s a different world, yet no measurement could tell it apart from ours.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-05.text: The shift leaves every distance between the bodies unchanged. For Leibniz, therefore, nothing about the world has changed.

metaphysics-being-41/beat-07.text: Newton’s case for absolute space rested on rotation. Water in a spinning vessel rises up the sides, even when it’s still relative to the vessel.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-00.text: Leibniz asked why there is something rather than nothing. Martin Heidegger later called it the first of all questions.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-01.text: Heidegger calls this the fundamental question of metaphysics. The question concerns beings as a whole, not why any one thing exists.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-02.text: It asks why there are any beings at all, the questioner included.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-03.text: Leibniz grounded the question in his principle of sufficient reason. It holds that every fact needs a reason.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-04.text: If every fact needs a reason, the existence of anything at all needs one too. What could that reason be?

metaphysics-being-5/beat-06.text: The questioner is also part of the question. You’re a being for whom your own being is an issue.

metaphysics-being-5/beat-07.text: Heidegger calls such a being Dasein, German for “being-there”. It’s the being that can inquire into being itself.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-00.text: Suppose every plank of a ship is replaced, one at a time. When no original wood remains, is it the same ship?

metaphysics-being-6/beat-01.text: Plutarch reports that the Athenians preserved the ship of Theseus, replacing decayed timbers with new ones.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-02.text: Plutarch adds that philosophers disputed whether it remained the same ship.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-04.text: Philosophers distinguish two senses of the word “same”. Two new coins can be qualitatively identical, sharing every feature.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-05.text: Numerical identity is being one and the same thing over time. The repaired ship seems to keep numerical identity even as its material changes.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-06.text: The same puzzle applies to you. Most of your cells have been replaced since you were a young child.

metaphysics-being-6/beat-07.text: Yet you still regard that child as numerically identical to yourself.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-00.text: You only ever experience the present moment. You never directly feel yesterday or tomorrow.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-01.text: This raises a metaphysical question. Do past and future moments exist, or only the present one?

metaphysics-being-7/beat-02.text: Consider time as a line running from earlier to later, with three moments marked: yesterday, now and tomorrow.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-03.text: On this picture, the moments look like places, each as real as the others.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-04.text: Suppose only the present exists. Then yesterday has no place on the line, and its frame is empty.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-05.text: On this view, the past isn’t stored somewhere else. It no longer exists at all.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-06.text: The future is in the same position. Tomorrow doesn’t exist yet.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-07.text: So its frame is empty too, because that moment hasn’t yet occurred.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-08.text: This view is called presentism: only present things exist.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-09.text: For the presentist, reality consists of a single moment, and which moment that is keeps changing.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-10.text: A rival theory of time rejects this picture. It compares time to a printed book.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-11.text: Page four hundred is as fully printed as page one. Where you happen to be reading makes no page more real.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-13.text: This view is called eternalism. Past, present and future moments all exist, forming a block universe.

metaphysics-being-7/beat-14.text: On this view, the word “now” works like the word “here”. Each marks the speaker’s position, not a privileged part of reality.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-00.text: Consider the last choice you made. Could events long before your birth have already made it inevitable?

metaphysics-being-8/beat-01.text: Determinism holds that every event is fixed by earlier events and the laws of nature.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-02.text: The causes of your choice began before you existed: your genes, your parents, your upbringing. Each state of the world produced the next.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-03.text: That chain of causes leads, step by step, to the choice you made.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-04.text: Hard determinism says nobody is ever free. Everything you do was fixed by what came before, so you could not have done otherwise.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-05.text: On this view, no choice you’ve ever made could have gone differently.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-06.text: Your own choice is one more event in the chain, fixed by the events before it.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-07.text: Even your proudest choices were settled by causes that began long before your birth.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-08.text: A second position denies that choices are determined. A free choice, it holds, begins a new chain that no earlier cause fixed.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-09.text: This is libertarian free will, which is distinct from political libertarianism.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-10.text: A third position rejects an assumption both sides share: that freedom requires uncaused choices.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-11.text: On this view, being caused is compatible with being free. What, then, makes a choice free?

metaphysics-being-8/beat-14.text: This position is called compatibilism. David Hume and, later, Harry Frankfurt held that free will is compatible with determinism.

metaphysics-being-8/beat-15.text: For Hume, you act freely when your action comes from your own will, not from external constraint.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-00.text: A human brain weighs about three pounds and occupies space. Does a thought, such as the one you’re having now, weigh anything?

metaphysics-being-9/beat-01.text: Descartes argued that mind and body are distinct substances. Mind thinks and takes up no space, and body takes up space and doesn’t think.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-02.text: This view is called substance dualism. On it, the mind could exist without the body.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-04.text: Suppose you decide to lift your arm. Then something with no size or location must cause a physical limb to move.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-05.text: Descartes put the link in the pineal gland. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia objected: moving a body takes contact, and a mind with no extension cannot touch it.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-06.text: Physicalists hold that the mind is physical, so there’s no gap to cross. Brain damage can alter memory, mood and even character.

metaphysics-being-9/beat-07.text: This evidence suggests that the mind isn’t a separate substance. It is something the brain does, the way digestion is something the gut does.

political-political-1/beat-00.text: Every state claims authority over you, although you never agreed to its rules. Why, then, should you obey?

political-political-1/beat-01.text: This is the problem of political authority. What could give a state the right to rule?

political-political-1/beat-02.text: Thomas Hobbes asks you to imagine life without any law, court or ruler. This condition is called the state of nature.

political-political-1/beat-03.text: With no common power to settle disputes, people compete and distrust one another. Hobbes says such a life is “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”.

political-political-1/beat-04.text: Even the weakest can kill the strongest, so fear gives everyone a reason to strike first. Hobbes calls the result a war “of every man against every man”.

political-political-1/beat-05.text: Hobbes argues that the only escape is a covenant. In it, everyone authorises one sovereign to keep the peace.

political-political-1/beat-08.text: No one ever signed such a contract, and no one needs to. The contract is a test of legitimacy, not a document.

political-political-1/beat-09.text: For Hobbes, subjects have no right to rebel against the sovereign they authorised. John Locke disagreed: a people may resist rulers who violate their rights.

political-political-10/beat-00.text: Consider three people whose holdings differ: the largest pile is three times the smallest. Is that distribution unjust?

political-political-10/beat-01.text: The sizes of the piles alone don’t settle the question. Locke, Nozick and Rawls each look for something different.

political-political-10/beat-02.text: John Locke begins before anything is owned. In his account, the earth is first given to humankind in common.

political-political-10/beat-03.text: You own your labour, so land you mix your labour with becomes yours. Locke adds a proviso: enough, and as good, must be left for others.

political-political-10/beat-04.text: So every holding has a history as well as a size. The history records how it was acquired and passed on.

political-political-10/beat-05.text: This one was taken from common land, traded twice and then given as a gift.

political-political-10/beat-06.text: Robert Nozick looks only at this history. He asks whether the first taking was just and every transfer free.

political-political-10/beat-07.text: If every step was just, Nozick holds, the final holding is just, however large.

political-political-10/beat-09.text: John Rawls judges the distribution rather than its history. He asks how well the least advantaged fare.

political-political-10/beat-10.text: Rawls permits inequality only if it improves the position of whoever is worst off.

political-political-11/beat-00.text: Suppose there were no government: no courts, no police and no one in charge. How would people behave?

political-political-11/beat-01.text: Your answer largely determines which state you can justify.

political-political-11/beat-02.text: Political philosophers call this condition the state of nature. Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau each assume a view of human nature and ask what state it requires.

political-political-11/beat-03.text: Thomas Hobbes reads human nature as fearful. People are roughly equal in strength, so anyone can kill anyone, and each has reason to strike first.

political-political-11/beat-04.text: Only a sovereign above every subject can end this war. Hobbes holds that the sovereign’s power must be absolute.

political-political-11/beat-06.text: John Locke reads human nature as rational. People already have duties under natural law, and what they lack is an impartial judge.

political-political-11/beat-07.text: So Locke’s government is limited, and the people keep the natural rights they held before it existed.

political-political-11/beat-08.text: Rousseau reads human nature as innocent. People lived at peace until property and rank made them compare themselves.

political-political-11/beat-09.text: In Rousseau’s state, no ruler stands above the people. Everybody is bound to the common good, as expressed in the general will.

political-political-11/beat-10.text: Rousseau argues that by obeying the general will, each person obeys only himself and remains free.

political-political-12/beat-00.text: Rousseau wrote that a citizen who refuses to obey the general will must be forced to be free. The phrase seems contradictory.

political-political-12/beat-01.text: In his 1958 lecture on liberty, Isaiah Berlin explains how the phrase can make sense, and why that’s dangerous.

political-political-12/beat-02.text: One question asks how many doors are open to you, with no one blocking them. That is negative liberty, and it is entirely about what other people are doing.

political-political-12/beat-03.text: With the door open and no one blocking it, you enjoy negative liberty.

political-political-12/beat-04.text: The definition says nothing about whether you can walk through the door.

political-political-12/beat-06.text: Positive liberty is self-mastery. Berlin warns that a regime may claim your real self wants what the regime plans.

political-political-12/beat-07.text: The regime then removes your choices and calls the result freedom, because it serves your supposed real self.

political-political-13/beat-00.text: John Stuart Mill accepts only one reason for coercing a person against their will. The reason is to prevent harm to others.

political-political-13/beat-01.text: Mill rejects coercion for a person’s own good, and coercion merely because others dislike the choice.

political-political-13/beat-02.text: Suppose a speaker says something most of the town finds repellent. No one is assaulted, robbed or threatened.

political-political-13/beat-03.text: The town argues that the speaker should be stopped.

political-political-13/beat-04.text: The argument has three steps, and read in order it appears valid.

political-political-13/beat-05.text: Each step seems to follow from the one before, and the conclusion is the one the town wanted.

political-political-13/beat-07.text: Mill accepts the first step, because the townspeople are offended. He also accepts the third, because it restates his own principle.

political-political-13/beat-08.text: So the town’s whole case depends on the middle step.

political-political-14/beat-00.text: Robert Nozick asks you to start from any distribution you consider just, even an equal one. Letting you choose makes the argument apply to every pattern.

political-political-14/beat-01.text: Suppose a basketball star agrees to play if twenty-five cents of each ticket goes to him. In a season, a million people pay to watch.

political-political-14/beat-02.text: Every single transfer is free. Each spectator chooses to pay, and the star chooses to play.

political-political-14/beat-03.text: The original pattern is now gone. The star has a quarter of a million dollars more, yet no one was wronged at any step.

political-political-14/beat-05.text: To restore the original pattern, something in this sequence must be stopped. Nozick asks which stage you’d stop.

political-political-15/beat-00.text: Breaking a law can be the most law-respecting thing a person does. Martin Luther King Jr. argued so, but only under strict conditions.

political-political-15/beat-01.text: First, a clear and serious wrong must be found. Second, lawful routes must be tried, such as petitions, courts and elections.

political-political-15/beat-02.text: John Rawls treats civil disobedience as a last resort, justified only after lawful appeals have failed.

political-political-15/beat-03.text: Third, the law is broken openly and without violence. Fourth, the lawbreaker stays and accepts the legal penalty.

political-political-15/beat-05.text: Consider a protest that names the injustice, tries the courts and breaks the law openly, then leaves to avoid arrest. It meets three of the four conditions.

political-political-16/beat-00.text: Suppose you fit the same bolt all day on an assembly line. Karl Marx argues that work connects a person to four things.

political-political-16/beat-01.text: These are the product, the activity of working, your human potential and your fellow workers.

political-political-16/beat-02.text: The car you help build belongs to the company, and you couldn’t afford one. The line sets the pace and you cannot stop it.

political-political-16/beat-03.text: So the worker is separated from both the product and the activity of working.

political-political-16/beat-04.text: Two more kinds of split follow. Doing the same task again and again leaves no room to create, and coworkers become rivals for the same jobs.

political-political-16/beat-06.text: Marx argues that none of this depends on the wage. It follows from who owns the means of production and who controls the work.

political-political-17/beat-00.text: Consider a village that digs a well together and keeps a rota for hauling water. Everyone takes a turn and everyone drinks, but no one signed an agreement.

political-political-17/beat-01.text: A newcomer drinks from the well daily, but his row on the rota is empty. When his turn comes, he says he never agreed to haul.

political-political-17/beat-02.text: The newcomer is right that he never consented. Almost no citizen has ever given express consent to the state either, which is a problem for consent theories.

political-political-17/beat-04.text: So fair play stops asking about signatures. Hart argued that people who benefit from a shared scheme owe a share of the burdens.

political-political-18/beat-00.text: Consider two people who each receive an identical bicycle. In terms of resources, the two are equal.

political-political-18/beat-01.text: Both set off, and one rider crosses the whole city.

political-political-18/beat-02.text: The other rider cannot use his legs, so the bicycle takes him almost nowhere.

political-political-18/beat-03.text: The resource was equal at the start, yet it produced very different amounts of mobility.

political-political-18/beat-05.text: So Amartya Sen measures equality in a new way. He asks what people are able to do and be, and calls this their capabilities.

political-political-19/beat-00.text: Peter Singer asks you to suppose a child is drowning in a shallow pond at your feet. Saving the child will ruin your shoes.

political-political-19/beat-01.text: The cost of helping is the price of the shoes, and that cost stays the same at any distance.

political-political-19/beat-02.text: The sense that you must act, however, weakens as the child gets farther away.

political-political-19/beat-03.text: Suppose the child is eight thousand miles away, and the same money would save them just as surely. Only your distance from the child has changed.

political-political-19/beat-06.text: The trouble is where that principle stops. Another death can always be prevented at the cost of one more possession.

political-political-2/beat-00.text: Force can compel obedience. Can force alone make people accept that a command is rightful?

political-political-2/beat-01.text: Power controls bodies through the threat of force. Authority also commands minds, because the people who obey accept it as rightful.

political-political-2/beat-02.text: Max Weber distinguished power from authority. Power is carrying out your will despite resistance, as a mugger does.

political-political-2/beat-03.text: Authority is power that people accept as legitimate. They obey because they believe the ruler is entitled to command.

political-political-2/beat-04.text: Augustine tells of a pirate captured by Alexander the Great. The pirate said that a lone ship makes a man a robber, while a whole fleet makes him an emperor.

political-political-2/beat-05.text: Without justice, Augustine says, a kingdom is a band of robbers. Both take by threat, and only legitimacy tells them apart.

political-political-2/beat-07.text: Weber named three sources of legitimate power. One kind rests on custom and birth, as in a hereditary monarchy.

political-political-2/beat-08.text: Charisma rests on devotion to one person. Rational-legal authority rests on law, so it stays with the office when the holder goes.

political-political-20/beat-00.text: Consider two neighbours, each with a complete view of how to live. John Rawls calls such a view a comprehensive doctrine.

political-political-20/beat-01.text: The two doctrines share almost nothing, and neither neighbour can persuade the other. Yet neither need have reasoned badly.

political-political-20/beat-02.text: Rawls held that free societies will always contain such disagreement, because reasonable people weigh hard questions differently.

political-political-20/beat-03.text: However, the neighbours share a street, and any law governing it will be enforced on both of them.

political-political-20/beat-04.text: The idea of public reason holds that such a law must be justifiable to everyone it binds. So its reasons can’t presuppose either neighbour’s doctrine.

political-political-20/beat-07.text: The reasons both can weigh are few. Almost everything each neighbour values stays within their own doctrine, and neither is asked to abandon it.

political-political-21/beat-00.text: Consent theory holds that a state’s authority rests on the agreement of the people it governs. Yet you’ve never signed such an agreement.

political-political-21/beat-01.text: One reply is tacit consent. John Locke argued that anyone who lives on a state’s territory thereby consents to obey its laws.

political-political-21/beat-02.text: The argument assumes you stay by choice, because you could leave. But every place you could move to is governed by another state.

political-political-21/beat-03.text: Leaving one state only places you under the authority of another.

political-political-21/beat-04.text: Almost all habitable land is claimed by some state. The open sea is unclaimed, but no one can make a home there.

political-political-21/beat-07.text: Philosophical anarchism draws a limited conclusion from such arguments. It does not call for revolt against the state.

political-political-21/beat-08.text: The view holds only that no existing state has earned the authority it claims. There may still be moral reasons to obey many particular laws.

political-political-22/beat-00.text: Consider a servant with a kind master. He never interferes with how she works, what she says or where she goes.

political-political-22/beat-01.text: Isaiah Berlin called the absence of interference negative liberty. By that standard, the servant is free.

political-political-22/beat-02.text: Yet he could interfere whenever he chose, and she couldn’t stop him. Philip Pettit calls such arbitrary power domination.

political-political-22/beat-03.text: If he chose, he could forbid her to work, speak or go out. She would have no means of stopping him.

political-political-22/beat-05.text: Negative liberty asks whether anyone is interfering with you now. Non-domination asks whether anyone could interfere at will.

political-political-22/beat-07.text: Kindness from the powerful can’t make her free, since it can be withdrawn. Pettit argues that freedom needs laws, rights and courts that check arbitrary power.

political-political-23/beat-00.text: Consider three things that define you. You chose two of them, a career and a club.

political-political-23/beat-01.text: The third, being a daughter, was true of you before you could make any choice.

political-political-23/beat-02.text: John Rawls asks you to choose principles of justice behind a veil of ignorance. You set aside knowledge of your class, your talents and your conception of the good.

political-political-23/beat-03.text: Michael Sandel calls the liberal picture of the person the unencumbered self. On this picture, the self exists prior to the ends it chooses.

political-political-23/beat-05.text: Sandel replies that the self is partly made of its attachments. Behind them stands no separate chooser.

political-political-23/beat-07.text: Alasdair MacIntyre argues that morality only makes sense inside a tradition. Without one, a person has no way to judge what to value.

political-political-24/beat-00.text: Consider a minority language used in the courts, taught in the schools and spoken at home.

political-political-24/beat-01.text: Charles Taylor holds that identity is formed in dialogue with others. So due recognition is a vital human need, not a courtesy.

political-political-24/beat-02.text: Suppose the language is removed from courts and schools but tolerated at home. Over five generations, the number of speakers falls.

political-political-24/beat-04.text: Taylor argues that a demeaning picture reflected back by society does real damage. People may come to accept that picture of themselves.

political-political-24/beat-06.text: Taylor sees two demands in conflict. One is to treat everyone alike, and the other is to recognise each group’s way of life.

political-political-25/beat-00.text: The feminist slogan “the personal is political” dates from about 1970. It says that who does the housework is a matter of justice.

political-political-25/beat-01.text: Liberal political philosophy long drew a boundary between public life and the private home.

political-political-25/beat-02.text: Law, work and voting belonged to the public sphere, where questions of justice applied.

political-political-25/beat-03.text: Home life belonged to the private sphere. Its roles were treated as natural rather than as a matter of power.

political-political-25/beat-05.text: Feminist philosophers reply that public rules shape private life. Marriage law, work rules and benefits all structure the family.

political-political-25/beat-06.text: Suppose parental leave favours mothers and childcare costs more than a mother earns. Her decision to leave work looks private, but public policy shaped it.

political-political-25/beat-08.text: Susan Moller Okin turned John Rawls’s veil of ignorance on the family. If you didn’t know your sex, you’d want the household to be just.

political-political-26/beat-00.text: A vote can count millions of opinions without testing their reasons.

political-political-26/beat-01.text: The aggregative model treats democracy as a procedure for adding up the preferences people already have.

political-political-26/beat-02.text: Jürgen Habermas built a model of deliberation: legitimacy comes from the reasons citizens exchange before they decide.

political-political-26/beat-03.text: On Habermas’s view, a law is legitimate only if everyone it affects could agree to it in rational discussion.

political-political-26/beat-05.text: In a citizens’ assembly, citizens chosen by lot hear experts and discuss an issue for weeks. Many change their minds.

political-political-26/beat-07.text: Iris Marion Young objected that deliberation favours those who argue in a calm, formal style. By contrast, a vote gives each person the same weight.

political-political-27/beat-00.text: Pacifists hold that war is always wrong. Realists hold that moral rules don’t apply between states at war.

political-political-27/beat-01.text: Just war theory takes a middle position. It judges a war by two separate sets of tests.

political-political-27/beat-02.text: The first, jus ad bellum, asks whether going to war is justified. It requires a just cause, and war must be a last resort.

political-political-27/beat-03.text: The second, jus in bello, governs how war is fought. Combatants must not target civilians, and force must be proportionate to its military aim.

political-political-27/beat-05.text: Suppose an invaded country fights back, and then firebombs an enemy city to end the war sooner.

political-political-27/beat-07.text: Augustine argued that a war could be just. Aquinas later named three conditions: rightful authority, a just cause and right intention.

political-political-28/beat-00.text: A prison sentence takes years from a person’s life. If anyone else did this, it would be a crime.

political-political-28/beat-01.text: Punishment does on purpose what the law forbids everyone else. So the state needs a justification that no private person could give.

political-political-28/beat-02.text: Retributivism looks back to the crime. The offender deserves punishment because of what he did.

political-political-28/beat-03.text: Consequentialism looks forward. Punishment is justified if it deters crime, protects the public or reforms the offender.

political-political-28/beat-04.text: Suppose a town is rioting over a crime. Framing one innocent man would end the riot and save many lives.

political-political-28/beat-07.text: Michel Foucault set aside the question of whether prison is justified. In Discipline and Punish, he studied how prisons observe and discipline the people they hold.

political-political-29/beat-00.text: Your place of birth may be the most consequential piece of luck in your life.

political-political-29/beat-01.text: Suppose two babies are born on the same day, one in a wealthy democracy and one just across its border.

political-political-29/beat-02.text: Neither baby earned its side of the border. Joseph Carens calls citizenship the modern equivalent of feudal privilege.

political-political-29/beat-03.text: Like feudal rank, citizenship is an inherited status that shapes a life. Liberal states reject inherited rank among citizens.

political-political-29/beat-05.text: Michael Walzer defends the opposite view. A community is partly defined by its power to admit or refuse newcomers.

political-political-29/beat-07.text: For Walzer, admission and exclusion are at the core of self-determination. Without them, no community could keep its character.

political-political-3/beat-00.text: A gunman can make you obey. What, if anything, makes you owe obedience to a government?

political-political-3/beat-01.text: Power is the capacity to compel obedience. Legitimacy is the right to rule, which creates a duty to obey.

political-political-3/beat-02.text: Social contract theory begins with a state of nature, a condition with no government. Hobbes argued that without a common power, it becomes a state of war.

political-political-3/beat-03.text: Hobbes held that people escape the war by covenant, agreeing to set up a sovereign who keeps the peace.

political-political-3/beat-04.text: John Locke argued that people consent to government to protect their natural rights. Government holds power in trust, and loses the right to rule by breaking the trust.

political-political-3/beat-05.text: The American Declaration of Independence, in 1776, drew on Locke’s ideas of consent and natural rights.

political-political-3/beat-07.text: Jean-Jacques Rousseau based legitimacy on the general will, which aims at what serves everyone. The will of all is a sum of private wants.

political-political-3/beat-08.text: Citizens who obey the general will obey laws they made themselves. For Rousseau, real freedom is living under rules you give yourself.

political-political-30/beat-00.text: Theories of justice divide over their target: an ideal of perfect justice, or the removal of existing injustice.

political-political-30/beat-01.text: Ideal theory describes what perfect justice would require. John Rawls begins there and treats it as a guide to reform.

political-political-30/beat-02.text: Non-ideal theory begins from the world as it is. Amartya Sen argues that justice advances by removing manifest injustices.

political-political-30/beat-03.text: In Sen’s analogy, to judge one painting better than another, you do not first need the greatest painting there is.

political-political-30/beat-05.text: Sen argues that Adam Smith and Mary Wollstonecraft opposed slavery without needing to agree on perfect justice.

political-political-30/beat-07.text: Rawls holds that non-ideal theory needs an ideal. Without one, it lacks an aim by which to judge reforms.

political-political-31/beat-00.text: Consider a commons: a pasture that no one owns and everyone may use. Four herders have an equal right to graze animals on it.

political-political-31/beat-01.text: Suppose you add one more animal. You keep the whole gain from it, but the damage to the grass is shared by all four herders.

political-political-31/beat-02.text: For you, the gain outweighs your share of the cost, so adding the animal is rational.

political-political-31/beat-03.text: Every other herder reasons the same way. The pasture is stripped bare and all are worse off, though no one acted unreasonably.

political-political-31/beat-05.text: Each herder weighs the same calculation. The gain from one more animal is a whole unit, and the herder keeps all of it.

political-political-31/beat-06.text: The cost is also a whole unit. Four herders share it, so each bears only a quarter.

political-political-32/beat-00.text: Consider an election count. Each mark is one citizen’s vote, cast at some cost in time and effort.

political-political-32/beat-01.text: The result is declared. Removing any single mark from either pile wouldn’t have changed it.

political-political-32/beat-02.text: Your mark is no exception. In a large national election, one vote’s chance of deciding the result is tiny.

political-political-32/beat-03.text: Anthony Downs argued in 1957 that voting seems irrational. A vote’s tiny chance of deciding rarely repays its cost.

political-political-32/beat-05.text: But deciding the winner is not the only thing a mark can do. Each mark also shifts the margin.

political-political-33/beat-00.text: Every free society must decide how far to tolerate ideas and movements that oppose it.

political-political-33/beat-01.text: Unlimited tolerance lets every view in the door. Even a view that hates tolerance itself still gets heard and gets a fair say.

political-political-33/beat-02.text: Suppose a movement uses that freedom to abolish it. Karl Popper named this the paradox of tolerance in 1945.

political-political-33/beat-03.text: Unlimited tolerance can be used to end tolerance. Popper argues that the intolerant, left unchecked, destroy the tolerant.

political-political-33/beat-04.text: The opposite approach fails too. A society that shuts out every view it finds threatening has given up on tolerance.

political-political-33/beat-05.text: Deciding in advance which arguments may be heard is the very intolerance the policy set out to prevent.

political-political-33/beat-08.text: However, Popper’s test concerns conduct, not belief: whether a movement will meet its opponents in argument at all.

political-political-34/beat-00.text: Decisions can be taken at levels from the individual to all humanity. Each question is settled at one.

political-political-34/beat-01.text: Some cases are easy. Your breakfast affects only you, so you alone should decide it.

political-political-34/beat-02.text: Suppose a village dumps its waste into a river. The decision is local, but the pollution reaches downstream towns.

political-political-34/beat-03.text: The opposite error also occurs. A distant ministry setting one school’s timetable has authority but lacks local knowledge.

political-political-34/beat-06.text: That is subsidiarity, and it has two halves. The first assigns each decision to the lowest competent level.

political-political-34/beat-07.text: The second says a higher level should act when a problem’s effects exceed what a lower level can handle.

political-political-35/beat-00.text: Suppose three living people must choose a policy whose effects will last for centuries.

political-political-35/beat-01.text: Nine of the chairs belong to people who are not born yet. They’ll bear its effects without voting.

political-political-35/beat-03.text: So far this is an ordinary problem of weighing interests. Derek Parfit named a deeper difficulty the non-identity problem.

political-political-35/beat-04.text: A different policy changes how people live: where they work, whom they meet, and when to have children.

political-political-35/beat-05.text: Different children are therefore conceived. Which people exist in the future depends on the policy chosen.

political-political-35/beat-06.text: Under the reckless policy, a different set of future people is born.

political-political-35/beat-07.text: Had the careful policy been chosen instead, none of these particular people would ever have existed.

political-political-35/beat-10.text: Parfit replies that an outcome can be worse without being worse for anyone. That gives reason to avoid it.

political-political-36/beat-00.text: Consider a street at night. Behind each lit window, someone is doing something ordinary and lawful.

political-political-36/beat-02.text: The slogan “nothing to hide, nothing to fear” misses this cost. It falls on people who do nothing wrong.

political-political-36/beat-03.text: Jeremy Bentham designed the panopticon, a prison in which prisoners can never tell whether the guard is watching.

political-political-36/beat-04.text: The watchtower may therefore stand empty. The belief that someone might be watching does the work.

political-political-36/beat-07.text: Nothing here shows up in a statistic. No law is broken and no case is brought.

political-political-36/beat-08.text: This is called a chilling effect: the range of lawful things people are willing to do shrinks.

political-political-36/beat-09.text: On this view, privacy isn’t mainly about hiding secrets. It protects the freedom to act without being judged.

political-political-37/beat-00.text: Consider two citizens on election day. Each casts one ballot, and the two ballots count equally.

political-political-37/beat-01.text: Their political voices aren’t equal. One citizen can afford to be heard across the whole country.

political-political-37/beat-02.text: The other, without money for advertising, reaches only the people nearby.

political-political-37/beat-04.text: John Rawls distinguishes a liberty from its worth, which is a person’s ability to use it.

political-political-37/beat-05.text: Both citizens have equal political liberties but unequal power to use them. Rawls argues these liberties need fair value.

political-political-37/beat-08.text: The dispute persists because both sides appeal to liberty. One side defends the freedom to spend on speech.

political-political-37/beat-09.text: The other defends the fair value of every citizen’s political voice. They disagree about which liberty comes first.

political-political-37/beat-10.text: Democracies differ in how they regulate campaign money. Each rule reflects a view of what political equality requires.

political-political-38/beat-00.text: Suppose you elect a representative. Months later, a vote arises on an issue nobody raised during the campaign.

political-political-38/beat-01.text: Theories of representation disagree about how closely a representative must follow the voters’ wishes.

political-political-38/beat-02.text: A representative might owe voters obedience to their instructions, independent judgement, or loyalty to a party.

political-political-38/beat-04.text: In 1774, newly elected for Bristol, Edmund Burke told voters he would not be bound by their instructions.
