political-political-38/beat-05.text: In 1780 Burke, having lost support in Bristol, withdrew from the election there. Voters can still dismiss a trustee.

political-political-39/beat-00.text: Suppose a law passes by sixty votes to forty, and you voted against it.

political-political-39/beat-01.text: The law now binds you too. A count of votes alone doesn’t explain the losers’ duty to obey.

political-political-39/beat-02.text: Four reasons are offered for that duty, and three of them are genuine justifications.

political-political-39/beat-04.text: Power compels compliance. Authority, by contrast, gives a reason to obey even when no one is watching.

political-political-39/beat-05.text: John Locke defends majority rule itself. A body requiring unanimous consent could never act.

political-political-4/beat-00.text: Are you free when no one stops you, or only when you’re able to act? These are two ideas of freedom that support very different politics.

political-political-4/beat-01.text: Isaiah Berlin called the first idea negative liberty. It’s the area within which others don’t interfere with what you do.

political-political-4/beat-02.text: John Stuart Mill’s harm principle marks the boundary of that area. Power may be used against you only to prevent harm to others.

political-political-4/beat-03.text: Mill holds that eating badly, taking risks and voicing unpopular opinions are your own decisions. Others may reason with you, but not compel you.

political-political-4/beat-04.text: Poisoning a well, defrauding a buyer or throwing a punch harms other people. Mill allows coercion only against conduct of this kind.

political-political-4/beat-06.text: Berlin called the second idea positive liberty: being your own master. On this view, someone free of interference may still be too poor, ill or uneducated to act.

political-political-4/beat-07.text: So positive liberty can back a bigger role for the state. It helps people act, not just leave them alone.

political-political-40/beat-00.text: Suppose two willing people agree a fair price for a vote. Neither is poor, and neither is deceived.

political-political-40/beat-01.text: The usual objection to a market is that it favours the rich over the poor. That worry doesn’t apply to this sale.

political-political-40/beat-02.text: A second objection concerns the good itself rather than the fairness of the exchange.

political-political-40/beat-03.text: Some things are changed by being priced. A purchased vote no longer expresses a citizen’s own judgement.

political-political-40/beat-05.text: Michael Sandel describes firms that are paid to hold places in queues for congressional hearings. Everyone involved consents.

political-political-40/beat-07.text: A queue distributes places by a single criterion: who arrived first, and who was willing to wait.

political-political-41/beat-00.text: A constitution is a body of rules written in advance of the events it must govern.

political-political-41/beat-01.text: Some emergencies, such as a plague or an invasion, fall outside every rule written in advance.

political-political-41/beat-02.text: John Locke gave the executive a power to act where the law is silent. He called it prerogative.

political-political-41/beat-03.text: The power has an owner and a purpose. Its holder is the executive, and its purpose the public good.

political-political-41/beat-05.text: Locke’s reason is practical. Legislatures are large and slow, and often not in session when an emergency arrives.

political-political-41/beat-07.text: Locke limits the power to the public good, so the people can judge afterwards whether it was used well.

political-political-5/beat-00.text: What makes a whole society just? Plato asked this in the Republic twenty-four centuries ago, and the answer is still disputed.

political-political-5/beat-01.text: Plato describes a just city as one in which each class does its own work. No class meddles in the work of another.

political-political-5/beat-02.text: Philosopher-kings rule, because Plato holds that only they know the good. Guardians defend the city, and producers supply it.

political-political-5/beat-04.text: John Rawls approaches the question differently. He asks which principles you’d choose if you didn’t know your place in society.

political-political-5/beat-05.text: Behind this veil of ignorance, you don’t know your class, talents, wealth or luck. So you can’t choose rules that favour yourself.

political-political-5/beat-07.text: The central questions of political philosophy are connected. Thomas Hobbes asks why anyone should obey a government at all.

political-political-5/beat-08.text: Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau ask what makes a government legitimate. John Stuart Mill asks how far its power over the individual may extend.

political-political-5/beat-09.text: Plato and Rawls ask what justice itself requires of a whole society.

political-political-6/beat-00.text: Would you accept this society if you turned out to be its poorest member? John Rawls made that question part of his test for a just society.

political-political-6/beat-01.text: Behind the veil of ignorance, you choose principles without knowing your place in society. Rawls argues that this fair choice yields two principles, ranked in strict order.

political-political-6/beat-02.text: The first principle gives each person the same basic liberties. The second allows inequalities only if they help the worst off and attach to jobs open to all.

political-political-6/beat-04.text: Suppose a surgeon earns far more than a clerk. Rawls’s difference principle asks whether that gap helps the worst off.

political-political-6/beat-05.text: Higher pay is just if it draws talent that lifts the worst off above the equality line. Justice is judged by how the worst off fare, not the best off.

political-political-7/beat-00.text: You’re free to say what you think. Where does that right come from?

political-political-7/beat-01.text: Does a government grant it, or a written constitution?

political-political-7/beat-02.text: Or was the right yours before anyone voted on anything?

political-political-7/beat-03.text: John Locke’s answer is nature. Before any government exists, he argues, each person has a right to life, liberty and property.

political-political-7/beat-04.text: On this view, no one grants your rights. Government exists to protect rights you already have, not to create them.

political-political-7/beat-05.text: Another tradition locates rights in agreement. A right exists only where people have written down a rule, signed it and agreed to enforce it.

political-political-7/beat-06.text: On this view, a right that no law secures is only a wish that there were such a right.

political-political-7/beat-08.text: A thought experiment separates the two views. Suppose a government passes a law forbidding you to say what you think.

political-political-7/beat-09.text: The law is properly enacted, and the state enforces it.

political-political-7/beat-11.text: A law can destroy a right that exists on paper. It can’t remove a right that exists by nature.

political-political-7/beat-12.text: These are natural rights: rights you have just for being human. A government can violate one.

political-political-7/beat-13.text: What a government never granted, it cannot take away.

political-political-7/beat-15.text: The claim has consequences. Eighteenth-century thinkers proclaimed the rights of man, but most denied those rights to women.

political-political-7/beat-16.text: In 1792, Mary Wollstonecraft argued from reason. If reason grounds rights, women share them, because women reason too.

political-political-8/beat-00.text: Consider three people standing at a tall wooden fence.

political-political-8/beat-01.text: A match is being played on the far side, and all three want to watch. Everyone agrees that each of them should be able to.

political-political-8/beat-02.text: The agreement ends as soon as anyone asks what equal shares actually require.

political-political-8/beat-03.text: No one has wronged anyone here. The three differ in height through no choice of their own.

political-political-8/beat-04.text: The tallest sees the whole pitch. The other two see only the fence.

political-political-8/beat-05.text: There are three spare crates by the gate, one for each person.

political-political-8/beat-06.text: One crate each looks like the fairest possible division.

political-political-8/beat-07.text: Each person receives an identical crate. The shares are equal, and no one is favoured or left out.

political-political-8/beat-08.text: Yet the shortest person still can’t see over the fence.

political-political-8/beat-10.text: Nothing was added and nothing was taken away. The same three crates now sit where they make a difference.

political-political-8/beat-11.text: All three now see the match from the same eye level.

political-political-8/beat-13.text: So a demand for equality is incomplete until it states what should be equal.

political-political-8/beat-14.text: Should it be equal resources, equal opportunities or equal happiness?

political-political-8/beat-15.text: Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum look at what people can do. They call these capabilities: what a person is able to do or to be.

political-political-9/beat-00.text: Democracy is rule by the people. Consider five citizens: four want one thing, and the fifth wants something else.

political-political-9/beat-01.text: They hold an honest vote, and the result is four to one. Plato distrusted such votes: a ship needs a trained navigator, not a show of hands.

political-political-9/beat-02.text: In Plato’s analogy, a crew that chooses its captain by vote follows whoever flatters it best.

political-political-9/beat-03.text: The procedure worked. Everyone voted, the larger side won, and that side now forces its will on the smaller one.

political-political-9/beat-04.text: This is democracy working, not democracy failing. Alexis de Tocqueville called the danger the tyranny of the majority.

political-political-9/beat-06.text: Mill and Tocqueville both held that a majority’s power has limits no vote may cross. Constitutional rights enforced by courts express the same principle.
